course.title: History: How the Past Is Known
course.description: How historians turn traces into accounts: sources, evidence, time, cause and interpretation, learned through well-chosen cases from the ancient world to 1914. A first course; later courses cover periods and regions in depth.
course.audience: A curious adult with no special background. They have heard of Rome, the Reformation and the First World War but have not been taught how historians know what they know.

paragraphs: In 1799 French soldiers near Rashid, in the Nile delta, found a slab of dark stone carved with one decree in three scripts, and it was another twenty-three years before anyone could explain how the top band worked. Every piece of history starts from something like that slab. The past itself has gone, and what we have are the things it left behind, inscriptions and letters, tax lists and charters and later accounts, each made by particular people for purposes of their own and hardly any of them made for us.

History is the work of turning those traces into an account of what happened and why, and once we know what to ask of a trace, a good deal can be settled. An emperor's inscription listing his own deeds is weak evidence of what Romans thought of him, yet it is excellent evidence of how he wanted to be remembered. A vast army size reported by a writer from the side that beat it becomes a claim we can test against everything else known about the war.

The same questions explain why historians disagree, since two careful scholars can accept every date about the end of Roman rule in the West and still argue over whether it was a catastrophe or a transformation. Once you can tell a fact from an interpretation, you can see which parts of such a dispute are about the evidence and which are about how to weigh it, and you can say which reading deals more honestly with what does not fit.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what a source is evidence of, and weigh it by who made it and why.
You'll be able to place events on a timeline and compute intervals across the BCE/CE boundary.
You'll be able to separate the conditions, causes and trigger of an event.
You'll be able to tell a fact from an interpretation and see why historians differ.
You'll be able to build a qualified historical claim and name what would weaken it.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Logic and Reasoning.

modules.title: Sources and evidence
modules.description: A source is a trace left by people with their own reasons. Three ancient cases show how to ask what a source can and cannot tell us.

modules.title: Time, numbers and cause
modules.description: Placing events on a timeline, counting what a record counted, and separating the causes of an event from its conditions and its trigger.

modules.title: Interpretation and voice
modules.description: Why historians disagree about the same evidence, how an event's meaning changes after it, and whose voices the surviving record leaves out.

modules.title: Argument across the long run
modules.description: Cause at the scale of a world war, building a historical claim from evidence, and a map of the whole spine that later period courses will fill.

concepts.title: Source
concepts.summary: Anything made or left by people that a historian uses as evidence about the past.

concepts.title: Primary source
concepts.summary: A source made at the time being studied, or by someone who took part in it.

concepts.title: Secondary source
concepts.summary: A later account built from other sources.

concepts.title: Sourcing
concepts.summary: Asking who made a source, when, for what audience and for what purpose before asking what it says.

concepts.title: Purpose and audience
concepts.summary: The reason a source was made and the reader it was made for, which shape what it includes and leaves out.

concepts.title: Corroboration
concepts.summary: Checking a claim in one source against other, independent sources.

concepts.title: Survival
concepts.summary: What reaches us is not what existed but what was kept, copied or buried in the right way.

concepts.title: Silence
concepts.summary: The absence of a voice or a topic in the record, which can be a fact about the past or only about the evidence.

concepts.title: Source written by an enemy
concepts.summary: A source whose author fought, or wrote for people who fought, against the people described.

concepts.title: BCE and CE
concepts.summary: Years counted back from, and forward from, the traditional date of Jesus's birth; there is no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE.

concepts.title: Century
concepts.summary: The 5th century CE is 401 to 500; the 5th century BCE is 500 to 401 BCE.

concepts.title: Periodisation
concepts.summary: Dividing the past into named stretches such as 'ancient' and 'medieval', which are labels chosen by later people.

concepts.title: Purpose of a record
concepts.summary: A tally is made to answer a particular question for its makers, such as who owes tax, and counts what that question needs.

concepts.title: Estimate
concepts.summary: A number reached by reasoning from partial evidence, which should be given with its range.

concepts.title: Proxy
concepts.summary: A measurable thing used to stand in for something not recorded directly.

concepts.title: Condition
concepts.summary: A background state that made an event possible without making it happen.

concepts.title: Trigger
concepts.summary: The event that set off something already likely.

concepts.title: Counterfactual test
concepts.summary: Asking what would likely have happened if one factor had been absent, to judge how much it mattered.

concepts.title: Interpretation
concepts.summary: An account that selects facts and weighs them to explain what happened.

concepts.title: Historiography
concepts.summary: The history of how historians have written about a topic.

concepts.title: Presentism
concepts.summary: Judging the past by present concerns as if people then shared them.

concepts.title: Significance
concepts.summary: How much an event matters, judged against a stated question and a stated audience.

concepts.title: Afterlife
concepts.summary: The later uses and meanings given to an event or text, often different from what it did at the time.

concepts.title: Anachronism
concepts.summary: Placing a later idea, word or thing in an earlier time.

concepts.title: Missing voices
concepts.summary: People who shaped events but left little in writing or were recorded only by others.

concepts.title: Reading against the grain
concepts.summary: Using a source for something its author did not mean to show.

concepts.title: Oral and later testimony
concepts.summary: Memory handed down or recorded later, valuable and different in its limits from a contemporary document.

concepts.title: Long-term cause
concepts.summary: A standing condition built up over years, such as alliances or rivalries.

concepts.title: Short-term cause
concepts.summary: A decision or event close in time to the outcome.

concepts.title: Contingency
concepts.summary: The idea that events could have gone otherwise because people chose and chance played a part.

concepts.title: Claim
concepts.summary: A statement that answers the historical question and can be argued with evidence.

concepts.title: Qualification
concepts.summary: A limit on a claim, such as 'in Britain' or 'mainly', that keeps it as strong as the evidence allows.

concepts.title: Counter-evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence a claim has to explain or concede.

concepts.title: Spine
concepts.summary: A chain of dated events and eras that lets later study hang off a fixed frame.

concepts.title: Thread
concepts.summary: A theme traced across many periods, such as writing, states, trade or belief.

concepts.title: Scale
concepts.summary: The size of the time or place a claim is about, which changes what evidence counts.

lessons.title: What a source is

lead.text: Look at the figure: the slab carries one text in three bands, and each band is a different way of writing. The top band is in **hieroglyphs**, the script of Egyptian temples, the middle band is in **Demotic**, the everyday script of Egypt, and the bottom band is in Greek, the language of the Ptolemies who ruled the country.

Why would priests have the same text cut three times? Because the decree itself says it should be set up in the writing of the temples, the writing of the country and the writing of the Greeks, which suggests that its makers were speaking to more than one audience at once.

afterFigure.text: We call anything that people made or left behind, and that a historian uses to learn about the past, a **source**. What makes something a source is not its age or its beauty but the fact that we put a question to it.

lead.text: It is tempting to treat a source as a window, so that looking through the Rosetta Stone we simply see Egypt in 196 BCE. The stone shows us only what its makers chose to say, in the way they chose to say it, and that is a much narrower thing.

So the useful habit is to ask, of any source, what it is *evidence of*. Suppose we ask what the priests said about their king in 196 BCE. The stone answers that directly, since it is their own text. Suppose we ask what ordinary Egyptian farmers thought of him. The stone is nearly silent, because the farmers had no part in it.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the object never changes while its value as evidence does.

reveal.text: The priests wrote the decree and the priests gained from several of the acts it lists, so it shows what they chose to credit the king with. It cannot confirm that he did it, because a text cannot check its own praise.

lead.text: A source made at the time being studied, or by someone who took part in the events, is called a **primary source**. The decree is one, for any question about Ptolemy V and his priests, because it was written in 196 BCE by people who were there. A later account that is built from other sources is a **secondary source**. A book published in 2020 about Ptolemaic Egypt is one, because its author was not there and worked from the decree and from other evidence.

The stone has a longer story than its decree. French soldiers found it in 1799 near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, in the Nile delta. It passed to the British after the French surrender in 1801 and has been in the British Museum since 1802. In 1822 the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced that he had worked out how hieroglyphs functioned, using the Greek text on the stone as one of his guides.

afterFigure.text: Each of these moments produced its own sources. The find, for instance, produced soldiers' reports, and those reports are first-hand evidence about the moment that made them.

reveal.text: The letter fits the definition, since its author took part in the handover and wrote in the same year. The word describes how close the source stands to the events, and says nothing yet about how far we can trust it.

It is a primary source for that question, since Champollion took part in the decipherment and wrote about it at the time. For a question about Ptolemy V it would be nothing of the kind, which is the point of the next screen.

lead.text: Champollion's announcement is primary for a question about how hieroglyphs were deciphered, but the same text is a late and distant account for a question about Ptolemy V, and it would be a poor guide to him. The 2020 book about Ptolemaic Egypt is secondary for the question of what Ptolemy V's priests wanted, yet it is *primary* for a question about how historians in the 2020s wrote about Egypt, because then it is itself a product of the time we are studying.

So we cannot sort a source into one pile for ever. We have to say what the question is first, and then ask two things about the source: was it made at the time of the events in the question, or by someone who took part, and did its author build it from other sources? A yes to the first makes it primary for that question, and a yes to the second, with no part in the events, makes it secondary.

Many people hear primary and take it to mean true, and secondary to mean doubtful, but neither follows. A priest's decree is primary and it praises the king in the way priests were expected to, while a careful modern book can be secondary and far more accurate about what actually happened. Primary tells us *where a source stands*, and how far to trust it is a different matter.

steps.headline: Classify a 2020 book on Ptolemaic Egypt for a question about the reign of Ptolemy V.

workedSteps.text: Start by writing the question down, because the label belongs to it. The question is: what happened in the reign of Ptolemy V?
Ask when the source was made. The book appeared in 2020, more than two thousand years after 196 BCE, so its author was not there.
Ask how the author knew. The author read the decree and other surviving evidence and built an account from them.
Both answers point the same way.

reveal.text: The textbook is itself an example of how people in the 1950s taught history, so for her question it is primary. The object has not changed, and the label has changed because the question did.
A primary source can be wrong, partial or one-sided. The decree praises a king in a priest's voice, and that voice is exactly what makes it good evidence of how priests spoke.

lessons.orientation: Say what a source is evidence of, and classify it as primary or secondary for a stated question.
lessons.nextAction: Ask who made a source, for whom and why, and use the answer to decide how far to trust each part of it.

blocks.text: What could a slab of stone tell us about the past? The Rosetta Stone, now in the British Museum, is a dark slab covered in three kinds of writing, and all three say the same thing: a decree issued by priests at Memphis in 196 BCE in the name of the young king Ptolemy V.

Before we read a word of the decree, we can already ask some useful questions of the slab itself. Who cut this text, and for whom? What do they want us to know, and what would they never think to mention?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a source is evidence of, and to classify it as primary or secondary for a particular question.
intro.whyItMatters: Every claim about the past rests on a source, so knowing what one can and cannot show comes before everything else.

recap.keyIdea: A source is evidence of something particular, and whether it is primary or secondary depends on the question we ask of it.

blocks.text: A source is anything made or left by people that we use as evidence, and it shows us what its makers chose to put there. A primary source stands inside the time being studied, a secondary source is a later account built from others, and the same text can be either one, as Champollion's announcement and a 2020 book both showed.
Primary does not mean true. It tells us where a source stands, and how far to trust it is a separate question.

lessons.title: Who made it, for whom and why

lead.text: Late in his life Augustus, the first Roman emperor, wrote a record of his achievements, and after he died in 14 CE it was set up on bronze pillars in front of his mausoleum in Rome. The text survives because it was copied elsewhere, and the best-preserved copy is an inscription at Ancyra, modern Ankara, in Latin with a Greek version. We call it the *Res Gestae*, which means the things done.

Who made it? Augustus, speaking in the first person. When? In his last years, and it was displayed after his death. For whom? The public, since pillars outside a tomb are read by passers-by. And why? To shape how people would remember him.

afterFigure.text: Asking these four questions before we use what a source says is called **sourcing**.

lead.text: Think about what Augustus was doing when he had his deeds set up in public. He was choosing, from a long career, the things he wanted to be remembered for, and telling them in the way that he wanted them told. We call the reason a source was made its **purpose**, and the purpose tells us which of the source's features were chosen.

The Res Gestae is excellent evidence of how Augustus wished to be seen, since it is his own presentation of himself. It is much weaker evidence of how his contemporaries saw him, because we hear none of them in it.

reveal.text: The sentence is Augustus's own telling, so it shows what he wanted known, and words such as liberty and tyranny are his judgements. The people who lived through those years are not in it, and theirs is the view that would test his.

lead.text: Tacitus wrote the *Annals* in the early second century CE, about a century after Augustus died, and the work begins with Augustus's last years and his death before going on to the emperors who followed him. He tells us he will write without anger or partiality, and that is a promise, which we can weigh but should not simply accept.

He can read many accounts and see how things turned out, which Augustus could not do, but he did not live through the events, and he writes as a Roman senator for readers like himself. The scholars who date the *Annals* place it only roughly, in the years after about 115 CE, so when we count the gap it is a rough count. If we take 116 CE as a round working date, the gap from Augustus's death in 14 CE is 102 years.

afterFigure.text: That gap is long enough for stories to have changed and for the writer's own day to colour how he saw the past.

reveal.text: Tacitus gives us the same years as told by someone outside Augustus's control, who knew what came afterwards. He is still a later writer who saw none of it, and he had a senator's view of emperors.
They are not independent. The second may simply have repeated the first, so their agreement is one report said twice and not two reports.

lead.text: When two accounts say the same thing, our confidence in the claim rises, and we call this **corroboration**. If witness A saw the event and witness B learned of it elsewhere, then two routes lead from the event to us, and it would be a coincidence for both to be mistaken in the same way. If B copied from A, there is only one route, and B's agreement adds nothing at all.

So the question to ask is not only whether sources agree but where each of them got its information. A claim made in one source alone is not necessarily false, but we hold it more loosely, and a claim found in several independent sources is much safer.

steps.headline: Source the Res Gestae with the four questions, and say what it is best evidence of.

workedSteps.text: Who made it? Augustus speaks in the first person, so the text is his own presentation.
When? It was finished in his last years and set up after his death.
For whom, and why? It was displayed in public in Rome, on pillars outside his tomb, and it lists his own achievements.
With the four answers in hand, we can say what the text is useful for.

lead.text: It is easy to conclude that a source with a purpose should be thrown away, and just as easy to conclude that an official source is neutral. A more useful habit asks what the source's makers could have known and what they had reason to bend.

Augustus knew what he had done and when, so his dates and offices are the part of the Res Gestae we might use with least suspicion, though we would still check them elsewhere. What he had every reason to bend was the judgement: why he did it and what people thought of it. An enemy's report is poor evidence of the other side's motives and may still be good evidence of what that enemy saw and feared.

reveal.text: The agreement corroborates the date, because the routes are separate: the government recorded the event for its own reasons and the traveller saw it for himself. A purpose does not spoil corroboration; copying does.

lessons.orientation: Source a text with four questions, and say what it is best evidence of.
lessons.reviewLabel: Who made it, for whom and why
lessons.nextAction: Reason about what the record leaves out, and treat a figure from a hostile source with care.

blocks.text: The Res Gestae begins with a title that tells us what the text claims to be: the deeds of the divine Augustus, by which he brought the whole world under the rule of the Roman people. Nobody could mistake it for a neutral list. It is a man summing up his own career, and it was cut in bronze where everyone in Rome could read it.

Does that make it worthless as evidence, or does it make it very good evidence of one particular thing? Answering that question for any text we meet is a skill, and it begins with four plain questions that we can put to a source before we believe a word of it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to source a text by asking who made it, for whom and why, and to say whether two agreeing sources really corroborate a claim.
intro.whyItMatters: A source can be trusted for some things and not for others, and you can only tell which if you know who made it and why.

recap.keyIdea: Ask who made a source, when, for whom and why, and count agreement as corroboration only when the sources are independent.

blocks.text: Sourcing turns a text into evidence of something particular: the Res Gestae shows how Augustus wished to be seen, and the Annals show how a senator a century later told the story. A purpose does not make a source useless, but it tells us which of its claims to check first.
Corroboration raises our confidence only when the sources reached the event by separate routes, so a copy adds nothing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what is missing from the record, and at how to treat a source written by an enemy.

lessons.title: Silences, survival and one-sided records

lead.text: Most of what we know about the war between the Persian empire and the Greek cities comes from Greek writers, and above all from Herodotus, who wrote in the fifth century BCE. He tells how a Persian force was beaten at Marathon in 490 BCE, how a small Greek force held the pass at Thermopylae and the Persian fleet was defeated at Salamis in 480 BCE, and how the Persian army was beaten again at Plataea in 479 BCE.

Where is the Persian side? We have the great inscription that Darius I had carved on a cliff at Behistun around 520 BCE, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, and it is a magnificent source for how a Persian king presented himself. It says nothing, though, about any war with Greece. What does not survive, as far as we know, is a narrative of the Greek expeditions told from the king's side.

afterFigure.text: So the story reaches us in the voice of the people who were nearly overrun and then won, and a historian has to remember that this is not the only voice that once told it.

reveal.text: Behistun was cut around 520 BCE, decades before Marathon, so it is excellent evidence for how Darius presented himself and no evidence about the expeditions to Greece. A Persian account of those expeditions, if one was ever written, has not survived.

lead.text: Think about everything that would have to happen for a Greek or Persian soldier's experience to reach a reader today. Someone had to record it, and most people never did, since writing was for a few. The record then had to be kept, and a papyrus roll left in a damp room does not last. It had to be copied by later hands, which happened only to texts that readers valued, and it had to be found and read.

We call what makes it through this chain its **survival**, and the practical lesson is that survival is not a fair sample. Stone and clay outlast papyrus, so inscriptions and tablets are over-represented. Texts that later schools admired were copied for centuries, and those that nobody wanted were lost. The widespread belief that the winners write history is too simple: survivors write it, and survivors include those who happened to be literate, to be rich enough to be recorded, and to have a text that someone chose to copy.

lead.text: When a source says nothing about something, we call that a **silence**, and the first rule about a silence is that it is not evidence that nothing happened. The Persian court's silence about Marathon does not show that Marathon was unimportant to Persia, and it does not show that Persia kept no records.

The better question is what the silence is a silence of. It might be loss, where a record was made and has gone. It might be that no record was ever made, because a defeat was not something a king chose to publicise. It might be that records exist in a form no one has read.

Herodotus gives the Persian army that crossed into Europe under Xerxes as 1,700,000 infantry, as well as 80,000 cavalry. He describes how it was counted: a space that held 10,000 men was packed, marked off, and filled again and again until the whole army had passed through, which he says took 170 fillings.

Herodotus was a Greek writer telling how Greece survived an invasion, and his story is better the larger the invader. The figure is also uncorroborated, since no Persian count survives and most later Greek writers depend on his. Most historians today think the real army was a small fraction of his figure, and the estimates differ widely. We call a source from the other side of a conflict a **hostile source**, and the right way to treat its number is as a claim to test.

His sum fits his own account, since 10,000 times 170 is 1,700,000, and whether the army was that size is a separate question. Most historians think it was a small fraction of his figure.

steps.headline: Assess Herodotus's figure of 1,700,000 for Xerxes's army.

workedSteps.text: Who gave it? A Greek writer in the fifth century BCE, writing about a war his own side won against an invader.
What could he know? What Greeks saw and heard, and what his informants told him.
Can it be checked? No Persian count survives, and the later Greek writers mostly follow him.
Last, consider what a number of that size did for the story he was telling.

reveal.text: The silence is real and the cause is open. A king recording his deeds chose what to record, so the silence may be a choice, but a historian needs a further source to say so.

blocks.text: Almost everything we know about the war between Persia and the Greek cities was written by Greeks. Herodotus tells us about Marathon in 490 BCE, about Thermopylae and Salamis in 480 BCE, and about the army of Xerxes, which he puts at 1,700,000 infantry. It is a gripping story, and it comes with a number that no one on the other side was ever recorded as checking.
What do we do with a story when only the winners seem to have told it, and what do we do with a number that makes the victory more remarkable?

intro.whyItMatters: Most of the past left no record that reached us, so knowing the shape of the gaps is part of knowing the evidence.

recap.keyIdea: What survives is a partial and uneven sample, so a silence must be questioned and a number from a hostile source tested.

blocks.text: The record we have passed through every stage of making, keeping, copying and reading, and each stage lost some of it, so a silence tells us about our evidence before it tells us about the past. We ask what it is a silence of, whether loss, choice or a record in a form we have not read.
A number from an author on the other side, such as Herodotus's 1,700,000, is a claim to test: we ask what he could know, what he had reason to inflate, and whether anything independent can check it.

lessons.title: Dates, eras and periods

reveal.text: The answer is 1. Each step along the line is one year, and the step that follows 1 BCE lands directly on 1 CE.

lead.text: Historians date events on a single line that runs through the birth-year convention. The years before it are counted as **BCE**, meaning before the common era, and they count down, so 44 BCE is earlier than 1 BCE. The years after it are **CE**, the common era, and they count up. The convention was set out centuries after the fact by a monk, Dionysius Exiguus, in the sixth century, and he started his count at 1 with no year 0.

That missing zero is the whole difficulty. Look at the figure: from 1 BCE to 1 CE is one year, since the very next year after 1 BCE is 1 CE. If there had been a year 0, the gap would have been two. A reader who treats the line like the ordinary number line will be a year out on every interval that crosses the boundary.

afterFigure.text: Where both dates sit on the same side of the boundary, nothing odd happens. We simply subtract the smaller number from the larger, taking care to notice which of the two is the earlier date on the BCE side.

lead.text: Suppose we want the years from 44 BCE to 14 CE, the span from Julius Caesar's assassination to Augustus's death. From 44 BCE down to 1 BCE is 43 years, since 44 minus 1 is 43. From 1 BCE to 14 CE is 14 years, because the step from 1 BCE to 1 CE counts as one and then 13 more take us to 14 CE. Adding them gives 43 plus 14, or 57 years.

A shortcut that does the same work is to add the two year numbers and subtract 1. For 44 BCE and 14 CE that is 44 plus 14 minus 1, which is 57 again. The subtraction is the missing year 0 showing up in the arithmetic, and if we forget it we get the tempting but wrong answer 58.

workedSteps.text: Split the span at the boundary. First go from 27 BCE to 1 BCE, which is 27 minus 1.
Then go from 1 BCE to 14 CE. The step to 1 CE is one year and 13 more reach 14 CE.
The two parts together make up the whole span from 27 BCE to 14 CE.

reveal.text: 196 plus 1799 is 1995, and subtracting 1 for the missing year gives 1994. The decree was almost two thousand years old when it was found.

lead.text: The year 1066 begins with 10, and it is natural to call it the 10th century. But the first century is the years 1 to 100, so the second is 101 to 200, and the century that contains a year is one more than the hundreds figure: 1066 is in the 11th century, and 476 is in the 5th.

On the BCE side the same naming holds, and the years inside it run backwards. The 1st century BCE is 100 BCE down to 1 BCE, and the 5th century BCE is 500 BCE down to 401 BCE. So 490 BCE, the year of Marathon, falls in the 5th century BCE, because the ordinal comes from the hundreds, and not from the direction of the count.

lead.text: Historians also divide time into **periods**, such as the ancient world and the Middle Ages, and the names turn out to be late additions. People living in the year 1000 did not know they were medieval. Scholars from the fifteenth century onward came to see the centuries between antiquity and their own day as a middle age, and the label stuck.

Where does the Roman Empire end? One common answer is 476, when the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by the commander Odoacer, and that year is also a conventional end of the ancient world. Another is 1453, when Constantinople, the capital of the eastern Roman Empire, fell to Mehmed II, a date often used to close the Middle Ages. Choosing 476 stresses the end of Roman government in the West, and choosing 1453 stresses the end of the Roman state in the East, so the choice is an argument about what mattered most.

blocks.text: Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE, and Augustus died in 14 CE. How many years lie between the two? It looks like a plain sum, but the two dates sit on opposite sides of the point where our numbering of years turns over, and before we trust any sum that crosses that point we need to know exactly how the count behaves there.
Every claim about what came before what, or how long something took, rests on this arithmetic.

blocks.text: Across the boundary we add the two distances and take off one for the missing year 0, so 44 BCE to 14 CE is 57 years. A year belongs to the century one more than its hundreds figure, so 1453 is in the 15th century and 490 BCE in the 5th century BCE.
Period names are later labels, and picking 476 or 1453 for the end of the Roman Empire is an argument about which part of Rome's story matters most.

lessons.title: Counting the past: records that count

lead.text: In 1085, at his Christmas court at Gloucester, William I ordered a survey of his kingdom, which his officials carried out in 1086. Its results survive in Domesday Book. The name comes from a later comparison: a writer in the twelfth century said its judgements were unalterable, like the Last Judgement, or doomsday.

For each place it says who held the land, how much of it was ploughland, how many tenants there were, and what it was worth, often at more than one date. The second view of the figure lists what the book leaves out. It lists heads of households and not everyone, it mostly passes over people without land, and some places, such as London and Winchester, are not in it.

afterFigure.text: None of this is a flaw. It becomes a problem only if we ask it a question it was never built to answer.

reveal.text: A household held several people, so the town had several times 1,200 people. The survey cannot say how many times, so the number of people has to be estimated, and that takes an assumption.

lead.text: Every record of counting has a purpose, and the purpose decides what is counted and what is left. A tax survey counts what can be taxed, a military list counts men who can fight, and a church register counts baptisms. None of them counts the whole population, and none was built for the questions a modern historian wants to ask.

That leaves us two sensible questions about any count. First, what did this record actually count: households, adult men, plough teams, payments? Second, what question can it answer well? A tax survey can tell us who held land and what it was worth for tax, and that is a firm use of it. Turning it into a figure for the population needs a further step, and the further step is where the care has to go.

Suppose a survey records 1,200 households in a town, and historians assume that a household held between 4 and 5 people. We call a figure reached in this way an **estimate**. At 4 people per household the town has 1,200 times 4, which is 4,800 people, and at 5 people per household it has 1,200 times 5, which is 6,000. The honest result is the range, 4,800 to 6,000.

The household multiplier is a convention, and historians debate it, so it matters which one is used. Notice too that the arithmetic gives a precise-looking answer from an uncertain input. A figure with many digits is not therefore an accurate one. Precision describes how finely a number is stated, and accuracy describes how close it is to the truth, and a careful historian reports the range and the assumption that produced it.

workedSteps.text: State what the record counted. It counted 900 households, not people.
At the low assumption of 4 people per household, multiply.
Now take the high assumption, 5 people per household.
Report both as a range, with the assumption that produced it.

reveal.text: The safe reading is the plain one: three villain tenants where there had been eight. The survey counted tenants because tenants owed dues, and it gives no cause for the change and no count of their families.

lead.text: Imagine a town of 4,000 people, which we invent to show the arithmetic. If 40 per cent died in a plague, the town lost 4,000 times 0.4, which is 1,600 people. If 30 per cent died, it lost 4,000 times 0.3, or 1,200. The two estimates differ by 400 people, and the only thing that changed was one assumption.

So when we read a historian's figure, the useful question is what it rests on. A figure that survives a change of reasonable assumptions is much more trustworthy than one that depends on a single choice.

reveal.text: The total rests on the 20 per cent. At 15 per cent the same county loses 1,800 instead of 2,400, so the question to ask is where the rate came from and how far the answer moves when it changes.

lead.text: The Black Death, which reached the port of Messina in 1347, killed very many people across Europe, yet nobody counted the dead. What survives are records made for other reasons: wills proved in a given year, clergy posts left vacant when a priest died, the deaths of tenants recorded on an estate, and tax lists from before and after.

A record used to stand in for what we cannot count directly is called a **proxy**. Each proxy covers a part of the population, such as clergy or tenants, and each has its own gaps, so historians build estimates by combining them and by judging how far each part stood for the whole. That is why mortality figures are reported as a range, and why they differ between regions.

A range shows how much of the answer is assumption. A single number would hide it and look more certain than the evidence allows.

blocks.text: Domesday Book looks like a census, and it is easy to quote it as one: so many manors, so many tenants, so many ploughs. It is better to ask first who wanted these things counted, and why. William I ordered the survey at Christmas in 1085, and what it counts is land, its holders and its worth.

A count is always a count of something. The skill of reading one is to work out what that something is, and then to say carefully what it can and cannot be made to show about the people who were never in its columns.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a record of counting actually counted, and to use an estimate with a stated range for questions the record was not built to answer.
intro.whyItMatters: Numbers from the past look firm, so it pays to know what each one counted and what is only an assumption.

recap.keyIdea: A record counts what its makers valued, and a figure built from it is an estimate whose range comes from its assumptions.

blocks.text: Domesday counts land and its worth, so it answers questions about landholding well and questions about the population only through estimates. An estimate multiplies a count by an assumption, so that 1,200 households give 4,800 to 6,000 people, and the range is the honest result.
Where nothing was counted at all, as with the Black Death, historians combine proxies, and the answer is again a range.

lessons.title: Causes, conditions and triggers

lead.text: Jan Hus, a Bohemian preacher who criticised the church, was burned at Constance on 6 July 1415. Johannes Gutenberg printed his Bible in Mainz about 1455. Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses are dated to 1517, traditionally to 31 October, although historians disagree about whether and how he posted them. In April 1521 Luther stood before the Diet, the assembly of the Holy Roman Empire, at Worms and refused to take back his writings.

Hus's attack on church practice came a generation before print, and the movement it began lasted in Bohemia without taking over Europe. Luther's came sixty-odd years after Gutenberg, and his writings were printed and passed from town to town within weeks.

reveal.text: The pattern is suggestive, since the movement with print spread much further than the one without it, but two cases fit several stories. To say what role print played we need the terms on the next screens.
It does not. The last event before an outcome is often only the one that set off conditions already in place.

lead.text: Historians sort the factors behind a large event into three kinds. **Conditions** are the background that makes the outcome possible: a printing trade, widespread discontent with the church, and rivalries between German rulers who resented the pope's claims. They do not produce an event on their own, since all of them existed for years without a Reformation.

**Causes** are the factors that actively push the outcome along. In this case they include Luther's own argument that people were saved by faith and not by purchase, and the rulers who chose to protect him, among them Frederick the Wise of Saxony. A **trigger** is the particular event that sets things off once the conditions and causes are in place. The sale of indulgences in 1517 is the usual candidate, because it was what moved Luther to write.

reveal.text: The price rise on that morning was the trigger. A trigger is the nearest event, and it is rarely the whole explanation, just as the sale of indulgences mattered because Luther, his readers and their rulers were ready to react.

lead.text: How can we tell whether print was a condition or a cause? One tool is to ask what would have happened without it. This is called a **counterfactual**: a claim about something that did not happen, used as a test and not as a story. We remove the factor in thought, keep everything else as it was, and ask whether the outcome still seems likely.

Take Hus. His ideas spread by manuscript and preaching, and the movement stayed largely within Bohemia. Take Luther. Without print, his argument might have been contained in the same way, though some historians think the demand for reform was strong enough to have found another route, and they dispute how much weight print deserves. So the answer is a judgement about likelihood, and not a certainty, and it still leaves us to decide which of the three kinds of factor print was.

steps.headline: Sort the printing press as a factor in the Reformation.

workedSteps.text: Ask what the factor did. It carried Luther's writings to many readers within weeks.
Ask whether it produced the argument. It did not: Luther's ideas on faith came from his own reading and thought.
Apply the counterfactual test. Without print, the argument might have reached far fewer readers, as Hus's did.
Those three answers are what we need to place print among the three kinds of factor.

reveal.text: It belongs with the causes. The sale and its preaching set Luther off, and this thesis is part of what he then argued, which pushed events along once readers took it up. Ask of any factor whether it was the background, the push or the spark.

lead.text: Suppose, as many historians argue, that without print Luther's protest would not have spread so widely. Then print was necessary for what happened, since the outcome needed it. But it was far from enough, because print had existed for sixty years before 1517 without a Reformation. The outcome needed the printing trade and the discontent, a message that people wanted, and rulers ready to shelter its author.

Events of this size have several factors, which work together and which were present at different times, and a historian's work is to sort them, say how each mattered, and argue for the weight she gives each one. Someone who names a single cause has usually stopped sorting too early.

reveal.text: The drought was necessary but not enough. A factor that was present many times without the outcome needs other factors beside it before anything happens.

blocks.text: In 1517 Martin Luther wrote ninety-five propositions against the sale of indulgences, and within a few years half of Germany was arguing about the church. Printing had been in use for about sixty years by then. Did printing cause the Reformation, or did it only carry a message that someone else had written?
The way to handle a question like that is to sort the factors by what kind of thing each one was.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort the factors behind an event into conditions, causes and a trigger, and test a cause by asking what would have changed without it.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every historical question asks why something happened, and a sorted answer is far more useful than a list.

recap.keyIdea: Conditions make an event possible, causes make it happen and a trigger sets it off, and a counterfactual tests how much each mattered.

blocks.text: For the Reformation, print and discontent were conditions, Luther's argument and princely protection were causes, and the sale of indulgences was the trigger. Removing a factor in thought, as a counterfactual, shows how far the outcome depended on it, though the answer is a judgement of likelihood.
A factor can be necessary without being enough, so a single named cause usually means the sorting stopped too early.

lessons.title: Why historians disagree

lead.text: The dispute is about what happened to the Roman West afterwards, and three famous books give three answers. Edward Gibbon, in the first volume of *The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire* in 1776, saw decay, and he wrote near the end of the work that he had described "the triumph of barbarism and religion". He blamed, among other things, the effects of Christianity.

Peter Brown, in *The World of Late Antiquity* in 1971, saw something else: a period of change in which religion, culture and ways of living were transformed, and which deserved study in its own right and not as a ruin. Bryan Ward-Perkins, in *The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization* in 2005, argued from archaeology that the West suffered a real material collapse. Use the buttons in the figure to see each in turn.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the three authors do not quarrel about 476. They quarrel about what to make of it, and about which evidence deserves most weight.

reveal.text: Over 229 years the questions, the evidence and the tools of historians changed a great deal, and Ward-Perkins could argue from archaeology that Gibbon never saw. The date 476 stayed where it was.
It is a fact claim: it names a date and an event that sources can confirm or correct. The next screen sets it beside two other kinds of statement.

lead.text: It helps to sort what historians say into three kinds. A **fact claim** says that something happened, and it can be checked against sources: the deposition in 476 is one. **Evidence** is the material offered to support a reading, such as the end of new Roman coin reaching Britain early in the fifth century, which Ward-Perkins uses in his argument. An **interpretation** is a claim about what the facts mean or why they happened, such as Gibbon's claim that Christianity weakened the empire.

A fact claim is challenged with a better source. Evidence is challenged by asking whether it is typical and whether it means what the author says. An interpretation is challenged by weighing it against rival readings of the same facts, and so it can be argued well or badly without being proved or disproved in one stroke.

reveal.text: It is an interpretation. Gibbon says what Christian preaching did to Roman society, and two historians who agreed on every sermon and every date could still reject that.

lead.text: Why do careful historians end up with different readings of the same evidence? Partly because they ask different questions. Gibbon asked why a great empire had come to ruin, and Brown asked what new world had grown from it. Partly because the evidence is patchy, and each author weighs it differently: pottery and coins speak of material life, and sermons and letters speak of belief. And partly because a word such as *decline* is itself a judgement, so two people can agree on every fact and still disagree about whether it applies.

Does disagreement mean that no view is better than another? It does not. A stronger interpretation covers more of the evidence, and it deals honestly with what does not fit. So the test of an interpretation is how well it handles the evidence and its rivals, and a historian who changes her mind because of a better argument is doing what the work requires.

steps.headline: Classify the statement: Fine pottery disappears from much of Britain in the fifth century.

workedSteps.text: Ask whether it names a thing that can be checked. Pottery finds can be dug up and dated, so it can be checked.
Ask whether it says what the thing means. It does not say why pottery vanished or what that shows about Roman life.
Ask how it is used. Ward-Perkins uses it to support the reading that living standards collapsed.
The three answers can now be set against the three kinds of statement.

lead.text: The study of how history has been written, and of how the questions have changed from one generation to the next, is called **historiography**. Gibbon belongs to it as much as to Roman history, since his book shows how an educated reader in the eighteenth century judged Christianity and civic life.

Reading the past through the standards and worries of the present, without noticing that we are doing it, is called **presentism**. The cure is not to pretend that we have no questions, since new questions are what bring new evidence into view. The cure is to say what our questions are, and to ask whether the people we study would have recognised them.

reveal.text: Her book is historiography. It treats earlier historians as evidence of their own time, which is why the same book can be both a study of Rome and a source for the eighteenth century.

They are not equally good. Here one reading fits the dates and the other fits none, so interpretations can be compared by how much of the evidence they cover and how well they handle what does not fit.

lessons.orientation: Tell a fact from an interpretation, and say what in a debate is about evidence and what is about weighing it.
lessons.nextAction: Distinguish what a document meant in its own time from the uses later made of it.

blocks.text: In 476 the last emperor in the West, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, was removed by a general called Odoacer. Yet some of the best historians of Rome have argued that what followed was a catastrophe, and others that it was a transformation, and they have read the same sources.
How can careful people read the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions, and does it mean that any reading is as good as another?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell a fact from an interpretation, and say what in a historical debate is about the evidence and what is about weighing it.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every book of history is an argument, and you read it better when you can see where the facts end and the interpretation begins.

recap.keyIdea: A fact can be checked, evidence is offered for a reading, and an interpretation, which can be stronger or weaker, says what the facts mean.

blocks.text: Gibbon in 1776, Brown in 1971 and Ward-Perkins in 2005 agree that the West changed after 476 and disagree about whether to call it decay, transformation or collapse. Their quarrel is about weighing the evidence, and an interpretation is stronger when it covers more of the evidence and deals with what does not fit.
Historiography studies how such questions change, and presentism warns that each age reads the past through its own concerns.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows a single document, Magna Carta, through the centuries to see how its meaning changed.

lessons.title: What it meant then and what it has meant since

reveal.text: It was a settlement of the grievances of barons against a king, and its protections reached the free, who were only some of the people in England.

lead.text: On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede beside the Thames, King John put his seal to a charter drawn up after rebel barons had risen against him. It answered their complaints about taxes, payments and the way the king treated those who held land from him, and it promised among much else that no free man would be seized or imprisoned except by "the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land", in a standard translation. The words "free man" mattered: that meant a minority of the population.

Pope Innocent III, whom John had asked for help, declared the charter null and void on 24 August 1215, and the war between the king and the barons went on. The first view of the figure marks the two dates, which are ten weeks apart, and shows how short the charter's first life was.

reveal.text: The clause protected free men, a minority of the population, and the charter that held it was annulled ten weeks after it was sealed. That is a narrow and short first life for words now so well known.

lead.text: After John died in 1216 the regents of his young son Henry III reissued it that year, and again in 1217, when it took the name Magna Carta, the great charter, to tell it apart from a smaller one issued alongside. Henry reissued it once more in 1225, in return for a grant of taxes, and this became the standard form. In 1297 Edward I confirmed it, and it entered the statute book.

More than three centuries later it had a new job. In the early seventeenth century lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke cited the charter against the claims of the Stuart kings, and the Petition of Right of 1628 appealed to it.

reveal.text: They tell us about the charter's second life. It was reissued, confirmed in 1297 and entered the statute book, and centuries later it was quoted against kings. That is real history, and it is the history of those later times.

lead.text: The distance between 1215 and the 1620s gives us two questions we must keep apart. What did the charter do in its own time, and what has it been taken to mean since? The first is answered from evidence about 1215. The second is a question about what we call the document's **afterlife**, the story of how later people used, remembered and reshaped it.

The danger is the slip into **anachronism**, which is attributing to a past time ideas, words or categories that belong to a later one. Reading Magna Carta in 1215 as a modern bill of rights for everyone is the standard example. The afterlife is real history, but it does not tell us what the barons meant. A later reading that differs from the original is not a falsehood. It is a piece of evidence about the later time.

reveal.text: The film commits an anachronism, putting a much later idea into 1215. The mistake matters most where a document has been famous for a long while and its later meanings are easy to read backwards.

lead.text: Was Magna Carta significant? If we ask whether it settled the quarrel between King John and the barons in 1215, its significance was small, since it was annulled that same summer. If we ask whether it shaped later claims about the limits of royal power, its significance was great, because it was reissued, confirmed and cited for centuries.

We call this a judgement of **significance**: a claim about how much an event or document mattered, for a stated question. Two historians may agree on every date about Magna Carta and still disagree about its significance, because they are answering different questions.

workedSteps.text: State the question first, because significance belongs to a question. Here it is the dispute between King John and the barons in 1215.
Gather the dates. It was sealed on 15 June and annulled on 24 August, which is 70 days.
That is ten weeks, a short first life for a charter now famous.
It was annulled and war continued, so for this question its significance was small. For a different question, such as its use by lawyers in the 1620s, it would be large.

reveal.text: It can be both. Significance depends on the question, and the treaty's later use as a model is part of its afterlife, just as the lawyers' use of Magna Carta is part of the charter's.

blocks.text: In June 1215 King John put his seal to a charter at Runnymede, and before the summer was out the pope had declared it void. Yet the same text, reissued and reshaped, was being quoted by lawyers four centuries later against another king, and people still invoke it today.
How can one document be both a failure and a foundation? It can be both because it had two lives, one in 1215 and one in the centuries after, and the evidence for each is different.

blocks.text: Magna Carta was a short-lived settlement with rebel barons in 1215, then a charter reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225 and confirmed in 1297, then a weapon for seventeenth-century lawyers. Reading the later meanings back into 1215 is an anachronism, though the afterlife is a legitimate subject in itself.
Its significance depends on the question: small for the dispute of 1215, large for later ideas about limits on royal power.

lessons.title: Whose voices survive

lead.text: The French colony of Saint-Domingue was the richest in the Caribbean, and its wealth rested on the labour of hundreds of thousands of enslaved people. In August 1791 an uprising began in the north of the colony. In 1793 the French commissioner Sonthonax proclaimed freedom for the enslaved in the north, and on 4 February 1794 the National Convention, the assembly then governing France, abolished slavery in all the French colonies. In 1802 Napoleon sent an army and moved to restore slavery. On 1 January 1804 independence was declared, and the new state took the name Haiti.

The events are well attested. What we want to ask now is who left records of them. The second view in the figure lists the main voices: planters, colonial officials, newspapers and the letters of Toussaint Louverture, the formerly enslaved leader who rose to command the colony's forces.

reveal.text: The memoir adds the voice of a leader, and one who had been enslaved, which makes it precious. Most of the people who made the revolution left no such account, so a history built only on the surviving writing would be told by those who held power or command.

Nothing directly. Having left no writing is a fact about the record, and it says nothing about what people thought or did. They acted, and acted at scale, and the record of their actions mostly comes from others.

lead.text: On one side are planters, officials, newspapers and leaders, whose words are plentiful. On the other are the enslaved men and women who made up most of the colony, who left few written accounts, partly because few of them had the chance to learn to read and write. Their words reach us when someone else wrote them down, in lists, reports and notices.

Historians use the word **subaltern** for groups outside the structures of power, whose voices are rarely in the official record. The term is a reminder that a large record is not the same as a representative one.

lead.text: Is the answer to give up? No, because a source can say more than its author meant. Take a planter's notice offering a reward for workers who had left an estate. The planter meant it as a claim of ownership and a request for their return. But the notice also shows that the workers had acted on their own, that they had left, and that enough of them had gone for the owner to pay to get them back.

Reading a source for what its author did not mean to say, and in some cases for the opposite of what the author meant, is called **reading against the grain**. It uses the planter's evidence for something the planter never intended, and it works best when we ask a question the author did not think to control.

steps.headline: Read, against the grain, a colonial official's report complaining that enslaved people were meeting at night on the estates without their owners' leave.

workedSteps.text: Say what the author meant. The official was warning his superiors and asking for stricter policing.
Ask what else the report shows, beyond what he meant it to show.
People were gathering at night, across estates and without leave, and taking real risks to do it. The meetings were their own decision.

lead.text: Some of the best-known scenes of the revolution come to us from later accounts. A ceremony held at a place called Bois Caïman, in the wooded hills of the north before the uprising, has become a central memory of the revolution, yet it rests mostly on accounts written long afterwards, and historians disagree about its details. That does not make it worthless. It makes it evidence of how people later remembered and told the beginning of their revolution.

Memory carried by speech, in songs, stories and rites, is called **oral evidence**. It is different from the written kind and it is not worse. It was made by people the written record often leaves out, and it can preserve what writing did not. It also changes in the telling, so we ask who told it, to whom and when, as we would with any other source.

reveal.text: The planter meant to report a loss, but the letter shows that the workers acted together and on their own. The author's purpose is not the limit of what a historian can learn from it.

blocks.text: In August 1791 enslaved men and women in the north of Saint-Domingue rose against their owners, and over the next thirteen years they overthrew French rule and founded the state of Haiti. It is one of the great turning points in the history of freedom, and yet almost every written account that survives from those years was made by someone who was not among the enslaved.
A historian who takes the sources as they come ends up telling the story of the people who held the pens. The question is what can be done about a record that is large, detailed and lopsided.

intro.whyItMatters: Whose voices a record carries decides whose history you can tell, so it is worth asking before you start.

recap.keyIdea: A large record can be lopsided, and historians read it against the grain and add oral and later evidence to hear the voices it leaves out.

blocks.text: The Haitian Revolution is well documented, but mostly by planters, officials, newspapers and its leaders, while the enslaved majority appear in other people's records. We name such groups subaltern, and we recover something of them by reading sources against the grain and by using oral and later evidence with care.
A gap in the written record is a fact about the record, and it is part of what we say about the past.

lead.text: On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot dead at Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. On 4 August, after German troops entered Belgium, Britain declared war on Germany.

The second view of the figure counts the days from the assassination as far as Austria-Hungary's declaration, which came on day 30. The declarations that followed all came within a week, which shows how fast the crisis moved once it began.

lead.text: Historians sort the causes of the war by the length of time over which they acted. **Long-term causes** built up over years: the system of alliances that divided Europe into two blocs, the race to build armies and navies, and nationalism, especially in the Balkans, where the borders of the Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires were under pressure. None of them was a war, and each made a war more likely.

**Short-term causes** are the decisions of the crisis itself: Austria-Hungary's demands on Serbia and its declaration of war, the mobilisations that followed, as armies were called up and readied for war, and the declarations of war in early August. The **trigger** is the spark, and for 1914 it is the shooting at Sarajevo.

lead.text: Does a long list of causes mean that war was bound to come? Many people at the time and since have thought so, but the word we need here is **contingency**, the idea that outcomes depend on particular choices and chances that could have been otherwise. In July 1914 governments chose between alternatives: to demand, to mobilise, to hold back, to declare. Different choices at any step might have limited the war.

Historians disagree about how much weight to give each level. Fritz Fischer argued in 1961 that German leaders bore the main responsibility, and Christopher Clark, in *The Sleepwalkers* in 2012, stressed that the decisions in several capitals interacted, so that the blame is shared. A counterfactual test, like the one in the Reformation lesson, helps us ask how likely a general war was without Sarajevo, and how likely it was had one decision been different.

Ask whether it was background or a spark. It was neither: it was a choice by a government, not a pressure built over years and not the first event.

blocks.text: On 28 June 1914 a young man shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne in the streets of Sarajevo. Five weeks later Britain was at war with Germany, and by then most of Europe was fighting. It is easy to say that one shot started the First World War, and it is just as easy to say that it was bound to happen anyway.
Which is it, and how would we decide? We start by fixing the order of events, since a cause cannot arrive after its effect, and then sort the factors by how long each had been acting.

intro.whyItMatters: A big event such as a world war shows how causes at different time scales fit together, and why none of them alone explains it.

recap.keyIdea: A war has long-term causes, short-term causes and a trigger, and because decisions in the crisis could have gone differently, likely does not mean inevitable.

blocks.text: For 1914, the alliances, the arms race and nationalism were long-term causes, the decisions of July were short-term causes, and the shooting at Sarajevo was the trigger. Historians disagree about the weight of each, as Fischer in 1961 and Clark in 2012 did.
Contingency is the reminder that the choices of those 37 days could have gone otherwise, so a likely war was not an inevitable one.

lessons.title: Building a historical claim

reveal.text: No finding could, because the sentence commits to nothing. A claim that is safe from every possible finding is also empty.

lead.text: Take a question that historians have argued over for a long time: why did industrial change come early to Britain? We could answer, "Industrialisation had many causes." It is true, and it is useless, because nothing could ever show it false. A claim earns its place by taking a risk. It says which factors mattered and how they worked, so that a reader knows what evidence would count for it and what would count against it.

A better answer, which we can use for the rest of the lesson, is this: Britain industrialised early because coal was cheap and wages were high, which made machines pay. It can be tested against prices, wages and dates, and it could turn out to be wrong, which is exactly why it is worth making. Robert Allen argued a case of this kind in 2009, and other historians have argued for the weight of trade, institutions, empire or ideas, so the claim is a position in a live debate.

In 1712 Thomas Newcomen's steam engine was in use pumping water from a mine. In 1769 James Watt patented a separate condenser that made the steam engine far more economical, and in 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened as a public railway using steam locomotives.

lead.text: Suppose we keep the claim about coal and wages. We now ask two things of it. First, what limits does it carry? A **qualification** is a word or phrase that says how far a claim reaches: that coal and wages were the main reasons, say, and not the only ones, or that the claim concerns Britain in the eighteenth century. A qualifier is not a hedge to avoid risk. It marks the true edge of what the evidence supports.

Second, what would count against it? We call evidence that points the other way **counter-evidence**. If steam engines had first spread where coal was dear, that would weaken the claim that cheap coal made them pay. A historian who names her counter-evidence in advance shows that she has looked for it, and a reader can judge how much it costs. The one thing that she must not do is hide it.

steps.headline: Build a claim about why industrial change came early to Britain.

workedSteps.text: Start from the question and propose an answer that names factors: coal was cheap and wages were high.
Test the draft. Could evidence show it wrong? Yes, prices and wages could be checked and could disagree.
Keep only the evidence that bears on it, such as the price of coal and the level of wages, and set aside what does not.
The claim now carries a qualifier: mainly, in Britain, in the eighteenth century. A claim also has to say what would count against it.

reveal.text: Counter-evidence is evidence of what the claim says should not happen. If industry grew fastest where there was little overseas trade, the link the claim proposes would fail.

lead.text: Piling up supporting evidence is the easy half of the work, and a long list does not by itself make a claim strong. A fact about the engine's speed may be interesting and still say nothing about wages. The test for each piece is whether, if the claim were false, we should expect to see it.

The harder half is the evidence that does not fit. A good historian says what it is and what it does to the claim. It may force a qualification, or show that a factor works only in some places, or lead to a different claim.

reveal.text: A qualification marks where the evidence ends. It is the opposite of a hedge, because it makes the claim exact.
Naming the town and limiting the claim is the better course. A claim that has not faced its counter-evidence has only been protected from it, and a reader who finds it will trust the claim less.

lessons.orientation: Turn a question into a qualified claim, choose evidence that bears on it, and name what would weaken it.

blocks.text: In 1709 Abraham Darby began smelting iron at Coalbrookdale with coke made from coal, and over the following century Britain became the first country to industrialise. Why Britain, and why then? Historians have argued about it for generations, pointing to cheap coal, high wages, trade, empire, institutions and ideas, and each of those answers is a claim that can be put to the evidence.
Some answers to a question like that are far more useful than others, even when all of them are true.

intro.whyItMatters: Every essay, argument and book in history rests on claims, and a strong one names its own weak point.

recap.keyIdea: A good claim is narrow enough to be wrong, carries a qualification, rests on evidence that bears on it, and names what would weaken it.

blocks.text: We built a claim about early industrialisation in Britain: that cheap coal and high wages made machines pay. The claim was narrow enough to be tested, the dates of 1709, 1712, 1769 and 1825 supplied evidence, and a qualification and a piece of counter-evidence marked its limits.
A claim that avoids its counter-evidence has only been protected from it, and a stronger one meets it.

lessons.title: The spine: a map of the past

lead.text: Marathon was fought in 490 BCE, and the Rosetta Stone's decree was issued in 196 BCE. Augustus died in 14 CE, and the last western emperor was deposed in 476. Domesday Book belongs to 1086 and Magna Carta to 1215, Luther's Theses to 1517, the uprising in Saint-Domingue to 1791 and the outbreak of the First World War to 1914.

The span from the first case to the last, from 490 BCE to 1914, is a good deal more than two thousand years, and the spacing shows how uneven our cases are. They reflect what we chose to study, and they do not reflect how much happened in each period.

lead.text: The Rosetta Stone, the Res Gestae and the Persian Wars taught us to ask what a source is evidence of, who made it and why, and what its silences leave out. Domesday and the dates taught us to read time and number with care: no year 0, centuries named by the next ordinal, and a count that records only what its makers wanted counted.

The Reformation and the war of 1914 taught cause: conditions, causes, short-term and long-term pressures, and a trigger. The end of the Roman West and Magna Carta taught interpretation, and the difference between what a document meant then and since. Haiti taught us to ask whose voices a record carries. The industrial claim showed how to build an argument that risks being wrong. Use the buttons in the figure to see the groups.

lead.text: A **thread** is a question that we keep asking across cases, and the course had several. One is *what did the record count or leave out?* Domesday counted land and left most people out. The planter's notice left out the workers' reasons. In each case the gap came from what the record's makers wanted or could do, and in each case the questions we asked had to allow for it.
Another thread is *who wrote the record?* Following a thread shows us the habit behind the cases, and it is the habit that carries to a new question, whatever the period.

steps.headline: Trace the thread who wrote the record through three cases.

workedSteps.text: Start with the Res Gestae. Augustus wrote about his own deeds, and he was the emperor.
Move to Domesday Book. The survey was ordered by a king and made by his officials.
Move to the Haitian Revolution. Most records are by planters, officials and leaders.
The three authors can now be set side by side.

reveal.text: The two events are 397 years apart and had different causes, yet both were explained with the same tools: conditions or long-term pressures, causes and decisions, and a trigger.

lead.text: It is tempting to take a vivid case and treat it as typical. A single event such as the sealing of Magna Carta can illustrate how a document's meaning changes, but it cannot show what the whole of the Middle Ages was like. A claim about an era needs many cases, chosen with some care, and a claim about a whole world needs cases from the whole world.
Most of our nine cases sit around the Mediterranean and in western Europe, with one in the Caribbean, because the course was built to teach a method. It is not a history of the world.

reveal.text: One case can support a claim about itself and suggest what to test elsewhere, but a claim about a whole century needs many cases. That is a point about scale.

blocks.text: Marathon was fought in 490 BCE and the First World War began in 1914, and between them lie the Rosetta decree, the death of Augustus, the end of the western emperors, Domesday Book, Magna Carta, Luther's Theses and the rising in Saint-Domingue. Drawn to scale on one line, those nine dates are spaced very unevenly: four fall in the ancient world, and three crowd into the last four centuries.
What does a line like that tell us, and what does it not?

recap.keyIdea: The cases fall on one line of more than two thousand years, each taught a move of the method, and threads such as who wrote the record connect them.

blocks.text: You can now place events across the BCE and CE boundary, ask what a source is evidence of and who made it, treat a silence or a count with care, sort causes, tell a fact from an interpretation, and build a claim that names its weak point. Following a thread such as who wrote the record shows the habit behind all of these.
The limits matter as much as the skills: one case cannot prove a claim about an era, and the sequence of one region is not the world's.

questions.prompt: Suppose that in 1801 a British officer who took charge of the stone wrote a letter describing the handover. For a question about how the stone passed to the British, what kind of source is his letter?
hints: Was the letter made at the time of the handover?
Did its author take part, or build an account from other sources?

acceptedIdeas: primary source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: primary source

questions.onCorrect: He took part and wrote at the time, so the letter is primary for that question. That says how close it stands to the events, and nothing yet about whether it is accurate.

misconceptions.feedback: A secondary source is a later account built from other sources. The officer took part in the handover and wrote about it that year.

questions.prompt: Champollion's 1822 announcement is used to answer the question of how hieroglyphs were deciphered. What kind of source is it for that question?
hints: Ask what the question is about, and when that happened.
Did Champollion take part in what the question asks about?

acceptedIdeas: A primary source, since Champollion took part in the decipherment and wrote about it at the time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A primary source, since Champollion took part in the decipherment and wrote about it at the time

questions.onCorrect: Champollion took part in the decipherment and wrote about it at the time, which makes his announcement primary for this question and not for one about Ptolemy V.

misconceptions.feedback: The decree is not what this question is about. The question asks how hieroglyphs were deciphered, and the announcement was written at that time by the man who did it.
A source is anything people made that a historian uses as evidence, and the announcement is evidence about the decipherment, which is exactly what the question asks about.

choices.label: Not a source at all, since it is about the stone and not about Egypt
A secondary source, since it was written more than two thousand years after the Rosetta Stone's decree
A primary source, since Champollion took part in the decipherment and wrote about it at the time

questions.prompt: A 2020 book on Ptolemaic Egypt, used for a question about Ptolemy V's reign, is what kind of source?
hints: Was the author alive in 196 BCE?
The author built the book from other evidence.

acceptedIdeas: secondary source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: secondary source

questions.onCorrect: A later account built from the decree and other evidence is secondary. The label belongs to this question about this reign.

misconceptions.feedback: The author was not there and worked from other sources, so for this question the book is a later account.

questions.prompt: Which statement about primary sources is correct?
hints: Think of the priests praising their king.
Ask what primary tells you and what it leaves open.

acceptedIdeas: Because they were made at the time, they can still be wrong or one-sided
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because they were made at the time, they can still be wrong or one-sided

choices.label: Because they were made at the time, they must have been written down
Because they were made at the time, they can be trusted on every point they make
Because they were made at the time, they can still be wrong or one-sided
Because they were made at the time, they must be official documents

questions.onCorrect: A primary source stands close to the events, but its makers had their own aims, and that has to be weighed.

misconceptions.feedback: A source made at the time can still be mistaken, or can leave things out on purpose. Primary says where the source stands, not how far it can be trusted.
Letters, diaries, photographs, coins and buildings can all be primary. Official status has nothing to do with it.
A coin, a ruin or a photograph can be primary too. The category is about when and by whom, not about the medium.
