E. A. Wallis Budge wrote a guide to the Rosetta Stone in 1913. It says of the inscription:

> The original form of the Decree is given by the Demotic section, and the Hieroglyphic and Greek versions were made from it.

A researcher wants to know how scholars of the 1910s explained the stone to the public. For her question, what kind of source is Budge's guide?
hints: Which years is her question about?
Was the guide made in those years, by one of the people she is studying?

acceptedIdeas: primary source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: primary source

questions.onCorrect: The guide belongs to the years she is studying, so it is primary for her question. For a question about Ptolemy V the same guide is a later account built from the stone.

misconceptions.feedback: It would be secondary for a question about Ptolemy V, since Budge wrote two thousand years later and worked from the stone. Her question is about the 1910s, and the guide was made then.

questions.prompt: A soldier's diary from a war records what he ate, what he feared before an attack and the rumours he heard about the generals' plans. Which question can the diary answer least well?
hints: For each question, ask whether the soldier could have known the answer himself.
A rumour that he heard and a plan that he never saw are different things.

acceptedIdeas: What the generals had in fact planned
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: What the generals had in fact planned

choices.label: What food reached his unit at the front
What the generals had in fact planned
What rumours ran among the soldiers
What he feared in the hours before an attack

questions.onCorrect: He could report the rumours and had no means of knowing the plans. A source is good evidence for what its maker could see or know, and weak evidence beyond that.

misconceptions.feedback: He ate the food and wrote it down at the time, so the diary stands close to this question.
The diary records the rumours as he heard them, and that is direct evidence that they were going round. Whether they were true is another matter.
Nobody stood closer to his fears than he did, and the diary is his own record of them.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How Augustus wanted the start of his career remembered

choices.label: That a faction oppressed Rome until Augustus freed it
How Augustus wanted the start of his career remembered
Nothing useful, since Augustus was praising himself
What the Romans of the time thought of his army and its commanders

questions.onCorrect: The sentence is his own telling, set up in public, so it shows the image he chose. Words such as liberty and tyranny are the part to test against other sources.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the claim the sentence makes, in the words of the man it flatters. Tyranny and liberty are his judgements on a civil war, and nothing in the sentence lets us hear the other side.
Self-praise limits what the sentence can prove about the republic. It remains his own account of how he wished to be seen, which is evidence of exactly that.
We hear one voice here, and it is the voice of Augustus. What other Romans thought would need a source made by them.

questions.prompt: A second chronicler, who is known to have read the first, repeats his report that a harvest failed in a certain year. What does the agreement of the two reports add?
hints: Where did the second chronicler get his information?
Count the routes that lead from the harvest to the two reports.

acceptedIdeas: Little or nothing, since the second may only be repeating the first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Little or nothing, since the second may only be repeating the first

questions.onCorrect: The agreement is one report said twice, so it adds no confidence beyond the first.

misconceptions.feedback: Two reports confirm a claim when each reached the event by its own route. The second chronicler read the first, so his agreement may be the same report said twice.
A chronicler can be good evidence for a harvest. The trouble here is narrower: the second account depends on the first, so it adds no separate route to the event.

choices.label: Nothing, since chroniclers cannot be trusted about harvests
Strong confirmation, since two chroniclers now both report the failure
Little or nothing, since the second may only be repeating the first

questions.prompt: Taking the four answers together, what is the Res Gestae best evidence of?
hints: Think of his purpose in setting it up in public.
Ask who the text was made for, and what he wanted them to take from it.

acceptedIdeas: How Augustus wished to be remembered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How Augustus wished to be remembered

questions.onCorrect: The text shows what he chose to put forward, which is what a reputation is made of.

misconceptions.feedback: The text is Augustus's own voice, set up for the public to read. We hear none of the public in it.
A text made for public display shows what its maker chose to show. His private thoughts are not in it.
The text is a selection of the deeds he chose to record, so it cannot be a neutral account of everything he did.

choices.label: How the people of Rome judged Augustus
How Augustus wished to be remembered
What Augustus privately thought of his own career
A neutral record of everything Augustus did

questions.prompt: A government inscription and a traveller's private letter, written without sight of it, give the same date for an event. What does their agreement add?
hints: Did either source copy the other?
Ask whether the routes to the event are separate.

acceptedIdeas: Corroboration, since each reached the event by its own route
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Corroboration, since each reached the event by its own route

questions.onCorrect: Separate routes make agreement count. The government's purpose does not spoil that, but copying would.

misconceptions.feedback: A purpose affects what an inscription is evidence of, but agreement is cancelled only when one source depended on the other. Ask whether that happened here.
Two independent sources raise our confidence, but they can still both be mistaken, so agreement stops short of proof.

choices.label: Corroboration, since each reached the event by its own route
Nothing, since the inscription had a purpose of its own and was made to serve it
Proof, since two different kinds of source agree on the same date

questions.prompt: These are two accounts of how Augustus came to power. Which part of Augustus's claim does Source B give a historian most reason to test?

extracts.text: I raised an army by means of which I restored liberty to the republic
extracts.when: written late in his life and set up in Rome after his death in 14 CE
extracts.kind: His own record of his deeds, displayed in public

extracts.text: Augustus won over the soldiers with gifts, the populace with cheap corn, and all men with the sweets of repose
extracts.who: Tacitus, Annals (translated by Church and Brodribb)
extracts.when: written about a century after Augustus died
extracts.kind: A history by a Roman senator, written for readers like himself

hints: Separate what Augustus says he did from what he says it meant.
On which point would the two writers contradict each other?

acceptedIdeas: That what he did restored liberty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That what he did restored liberty

choices.label: That Augustus had an army behind him
That what he did restored liberty
That he rose to power in Rome

questions.onCorrect: Augustus knew whether he had raised an army, and Tacitus agrees that he had soldiers behind him. Whether the result was liberty is a judgement, and Tacitus describes the same years as one man gathering every power to himself.

misconceptions.feedback: Both accounts have Augustus in control of soldiers, so on this point they agree. Agreement between an author and one of his critics makes this the safer part of the claim.
Neither account doubts it. Tacitus describes the same rise and disputes what it meant.

questions.prompt: A newspaper prints a reporter's account of a flood. In the following week three other papers reprint the account word for word. How many independent accounts of the flood does a historian have?
hints: Count the routes that lead from the flood to the printed pages.
Did any of the later papers send someone to see the flood?
A paper that reprints another paper's words saw nothing for itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three later papers copied the first, so there is 1 independent account.

questions.onCorrect: Four printings are still one report. Corroboration would need a second reporter, or a letter or record made by someone who saw the flood without reading the paper.

misconceptions.feedback: Four papers printed the account, but three of them copied it from the first. A copy adds no new route to the event.
The three reprints all go back to the first paper, so they add nothing of their own. Count the reports that reached the flood by their own route.

questions.prompt: A source plainly serves its author's purpose. What is the sound way to treat it?
hints: Ask what the author could have known.
Ask what the source is evidence of.

acceptedIdeas: Use it for what its author could have known, and test the rest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use it for what its author could have known, and test the rest

choices.label: Use it for what its author could have known, and test the rest
Trust it unless another source happens to contradict it on the point
Discard it, because its author had a purpose of their own
Trust it, because its author was there when it happened

questions.onCorrect: Bias is a reason to question a source more carefully, and the questioning tells us which parts to use.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves a source's purpose unexamined until something happens to contradict it. A source with a purpose has to be questioned before it is used.
A source with a purpose can still be good evidence of that purpose and of facts its author knew. Discarding it throws that away.
Being there is a reason to take a source seriously. It is no reason to believe all of it.

questions.prompt: No Persian court narrative of the war with Greece survives. What does that silence show about Persian record-keeping?
hints: List the ways a record could fail to reach us.
Does a gap in what survives tell you which of those happened?

acceptedIdeas: Nothing certain, since a record may simply have been lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing certain, since a record may simply have been lost

questions.onCorrect: A gap in what survives could mean loss, no narrative ever made, or a record in a form not yet read, so it is not a finding about the past.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing narrative may mean a record was made and lost, or kept as tablets that have not been read, as easily as that none was made. The silence alone cannot choose between these.
A king might leave a defeat out of his records because it mattered a great deal and he did not want it told. Silence does not measure importance.

choices.label: Nothing certain, since a record may simply have been lost
That the Persians thought the war too unimportant to record
That the Persians made no record of the war at all

questions.prompt: What did a Persian army of that size do for Herodotus's story of the war?
hints: Think of which side Herodotus belonged to, and which side won.
A figure can serve the story its author is telling.

acceptedIdeas: It made the Greek victory seem all the more remarkable
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It made the Greek victory seem all the more remarkable

questions.onCorrect: A big enemy makes a victory more remarkable, which gives the author a reason to enlarge the figure.

misconceptions.feedback: No Persian count survives to show that, and a large number is not the same thing as a carefully counted one.
Herodotus describes a method of counting, so the number does not show carelessness. Ask instead whose story the number belongs to.

choices.label: It made the Greek victory seem all the more remarkable
It showed that the Persians kept careful records of their numbers
It showed that the Greeks had been careless about counting

questions.prompt: A king's inscription lists his conquests and says nothing of a battle he lost. Which statement is sound?
hints: Name the possible causes of the silence.
What would settle which cause it was?

acceptedIdeas: The king may have left it out by choice, but another source must say so
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The king may have left it out by choice, but another source must say so

choices.label: The battle was too small for the king to bother recording among his conquests
The battle never happened, or the king would have listed it
The king may have left it out by choice, but another source must say so
The inscription is worthless, as it leaves out the king's defeats

questions.onCorrect: The silence has several possible causes, and only a further source can show which one applies.

misconceptions.feedback: A silence is not proof of absence. Other sources may record the battle.
The inscription is good evidence of what the king chose to show. Its limits do not make it worthless.
Nothing says the battle was small. A king might leave out a large defeat for exactly that reason.

questions.prompt:
Elsewhere in his history Herodotus says how he treats the stories he has heard, in G. C. Macaulay's translation.

> I however am bound to report that which is reported, though I am not bound altogether to believe it; and let this saying be considered to hold good as regards every narrative in the history

What does this tell a historian who uses his stories?
hints: Does he say that he believes what he reports?
If he is passing on what others said, whose claim is each story?

acceptedIdeas: That each is what he was told, and still a claim to test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That each is what he was told, and still a claim to test

choices.label: That he checked each story before he wrote it down in his history
That each is what he was told, and still a claim to test
That he doubted his informants and so invented freely

questions.onCorrect: Herodotus tells us he is a channel for other people's reports. Each story then needs the questions we would put to any source: who told it, what they could know and what they had reason to bend.

misconceptions.feedback: He says something close to the opposite: he reports what is reported, and he does not promise to have tested it.
Doubting a story is different from inventing one. He says he passes on what he was told, which makes each story a report from someone else.

questions.prompt: A general's report to his government gives the enemy's dead as 40,000 and his own as 200. No account from the enemy's side survives. In the terms of this lesson, what kind of source is his report for the enemy's losses?
hints: On which side of the conflict does the general stand?
What did the lesson call a source that reports on its own enemy?

acceptedIdeas: hostile source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hostile source

questions.onCorrect: The general could count his own dead and had reason to enlarge the enemy's, so his figure for them is a claim to test against anything independent.

misconceptions.feedback: It is primary, since he was there, but that says only where the report stands. The lesson has a name for a source that speaks about the other side in a conflict.

questions.prompt: Our calendar counts the years before the common era (BCE) down to 1 BCE, and then runs straight to 1 CE, the first year of the common era, with no year 0 between them. How many years are there from 1 BCE to 1 CE?
hints: Write the years in order: 2 BCE, 1 BCE, then the next one.
How many steps does it take to go from 1 BCE to the year after it?

acceptedIdeas: One year
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One year

questions.onCorrect: There is no year 0, so the two years are neighbours.

misconceptions.feedback: Two would be right if a year 0 sat between them. Without it, a single step along the line takes you from 1 BCE to 1 CE.
1 BCE and 1 CE are two different years, one on each side of the boundary, so going from the first to the second means moving along the line.

choices.label: None, since they are the same year
Two years
One year

questions.prompt: How many years are there from 27 BCE to 14 CE?
hints: Split the span at the boundary, as the two lines above do.
The two parts are already worked out. What do you do with them to get the whole span?
Add the years on the BCE side to the years on the CE side.
questions.onCorrect: Adding 27 and 14 gives 41, which is one too many because of the missing year 0.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 27 and 14 and forgets that there is no year 0. Take one off.
That subtracts the years as if both were CE. They lie on opposite sides of the boundary, so add.

questions.prompt: The decree was issued in 196 BCE and the stone was found in 1799. How many years lie between them?
hints: The dates lie on opposite sides of the boundary, so the span has two parts.
Find the distance from each date to the boundary, and remember that 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE.
Add the two distances. No year 0 lies between them to be counted.
questions.onCorrect: 1994 is the correct count, and it matches the figure of nearly two thousand years from the first lesson.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets that there is no year 0. Take one off.
That subtracts as if both were CE. They are on opposite sides of the boundary.

questions.prompt: Constantinople fell in 1453. What is the number of the century that contains 1453?
hints: The first century is 1 to 100.
Which century holds 1401 to 1500?
Add one to the hundreds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1453 lies between 1401 and 1500, which is the 15th century.

questions.onCorrect: The century number is one more than the hundreds figure of the year.

misconceptions.feedback: The digits 14 give the hundreds. The century that holds those years is the next number up.

questions.prompt: A historian is writing about the end of Roman government in the western provinces. She has to give the Roman Empire an end date, and the two common choices are the deposition of the last western emperor and the fall of Constantinople. Which year suits her subject?
hints: What ended in each of the two years the lesson gave?
Which of those endings is her book about?
The year you want is the one in which the last western emperor was deposed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Her subject is Roman government in the West, which ended when the last western emperor was deposed in 476.

questions.onCorrect: Choosing 476 stresses the end of Roman government in the West, which is her subject. A historian of Constantinople would have equal reason to choose 1453.

misconceptions.feedback: 1453 is the fall of Constantinople, the capital of the eastern Roman Empire. Her subject is the West, where Roman government had ended long before.

questions.prompt: Octavian took the name Augustus in 27 BCE, and the last emperor in the West was deposed in 476 CE. A textbook says that emperors ruled in the West for just over five centuries. Check the claim: how many years is it from 27 BCE to 476 CE?
hints: The two dates lie on opposite sides of the boundary, so the span has two parts.
Count from 27 BCE down to 1 BCE, then from 1 BCE up to 476 CE, and remember what is missing between 1 BCE and 1 CE.
Add the two parts. A span of just over five centuries should come out a little above 500.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 27 + 476 − 1 = 502, which is just over five centuries.

questions.onCorrect: The span is 502 years, so the textbook's just over five centuries holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the line as if it had a year 0. The step from 1 BCE to 1 CE is a single year.
That subtracts as if both dates were CE. They lie on opposite sides of the boundary, so the two distances add.

questions.prompt: A museum case holds five objects, and each label gives a date. In what order were the objects made?
hints: On the BCE side, is a larger year number earlier or later?
Write out the first and last years of the 3rd century BCE before you place that coin.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The years BCE count down, so 490 BCE comes first. The 3rd century BCE runs from 300 BCE down to 201 BCE, which puts that coin before the one of 44 BCE, and the two dates CE follow in rising order.

items: A coin struck in the 3rd century BCE
A map drawn in the 15th century CE

questions.onCorrect: On the BCE side the larger number is the earlier year, and the 3rd century BCE runs from 300 BCE down to 201 BCE.

questions.prompt: A historian chooses 1453 and not 476 as the end of the Roman Empire. She is mainly stressing:
hints: Which empire's capital fell in 1453?
Match each date to what it ended.

acceptedIdeas: The end of the Roman state in the East
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The end of the Roman state in the East

choices.label: The fall of the western emperor in the year 476
The first use of the word medieval
The sack of Rome by the Goths in the year 410
The end of the Roman state in the East

questions.onCorrect: Constantinople was the capital of the eastern Roman Empire, so 1453 marks the end of the Roman state there.

misconceptions.feedback: The word came later and is unconnected to either date.
The sack of Rome came in 410, before both dates, so it marks neither of them.
That is what 476 stresses. 1453 is the fall of Constantinople.

questions.prompt: A survey records 1,200 households in a town. Roughly how many people lived there?
hints: What did the survey count: people or households?
How many people usually lived in one household?

acceptedIdeas: Several times 1,200
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several times 1,200

questions.onCorrect: How many times larger depends on an assumption about household size, which is where the care has to go.

misconceptions.feedback: 1,200 is the number of households, and a household usually held several people, so the number of people was larger.
Each household held at least one person and usually several, so the town cannot have had fewer people than households.

choices.label: Fewer than 1,200, since several households often shared one home
About 1,200, since each household counts as one person
Several times 1,200

questions.prompt: At 5 people per household, how many people live in a town of 900 households?
hints: Multiply the number of households by the people in each.
900 times 5.
9 times 5, then add the zeros.
questions.onCorrect: 4,500 is the top of the range. The bottom, at four per household, is 3,600.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure at 4 per household. Use 5 here.
That adds the two numbers. Each household holds 5 people, so multiply.

questions.prompt:
No one counted the dead of the Black Death. In June 1349 the king of England sent an order to his sheriffs. It begins, in a translation published in 1915:

> Because a great part of the people, and especially of workmen and servants, late died of the pestilence, many seeing the necessity of masters, and great scarcity of servants, will not serve unless they may receive excessive wages

How can a historian use this order as a proxy for the deaths?
hints: What does the order say had happened to wages, and why?
A proxy stands in for a count. What can a shortage of workers stand in for?

acceptedIdeas: As a sign of scale, since the deaths had made labour scarce
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a sign of scale, since the deaths had made labour scarce

choices.label: As a count, since a great part gives the share who died in each place
As a sign of scale, since the deaths had made labour scarce
Not at all, since the king wrote it to hold wages down

questions.onCorrect: Workers were scarce enough in 1349 for the king to write to every sheriff, which is evidence that deaths were heavy among working people. It gives a sense of scale and no number, so it has to be set beside other proxies.

misconceptions.feedback: A great part is the king's phrase for many, and it is no measurement. The order cannot tell us whether a fifth died or a half.

The king's purpose shapes the wording, and excessive is his judgement. The shortage he complains of is still evidence, because an order to every sheriff makes little sense unless workers really were scarce.

questions.prompt: A historian studies one county in 1349. Wills suggest that 40 per cent of its people died, tenant records 50 per cent and clergy vacancies 45 per cent. How should she report her estimate?
hints: Ask what the three figures say about how sure we can be.
Ask what a single number would hide.

acceptedIdeas: As a range of 40 to 50 per cent, since the proxies disagree
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a range of 40 to 50 per cent, since the proxies disagree

choices.label: As a range of 40 to 50 per cent, since the proxies disagree
As 45 per cent, since it is the middle of the three figures
As 40 per cent, since the lowest figure is the safest to defend

questions.onCorrect: A range shows how much of the answer is assumption, which a single number would hide.

misconceptions.feedback: The middle of the three figures hides the disagreement between them. A single number makes the estimate look more certain than the evidence allows.
Choosing the lowest figure because it is safe picks one proxy and ignores the others. The estimate has to account for all three.

questions.prompt:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle describes the survey that William I ordered in 1085, in a translation of 1823. A hide was a measure of land.

> So very narrowly, indeed, did he commission them to trace it out, that there was not one single hide, nor a yard of land, nay, moreover (it is shameful to tell, though he thought it no shame to do it), not even an ox, nor a cow, nor a swine was there left, that was not set down in his writ.

What is this passage good evidence of?
hints: Find the words in which the writer gives his own opinion.
Whose view of the survey is this, and whose is missing?

acceptedIdeas: That a writer of the time thought the survey went too far
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That a writer of the time thought the survey went too far

choices.label: That the survey really did list every single animal in England
That a writer of the time thought the survey went too far
That the king's own officials were ashamed of the survey

questions.onCorrect: The words shameful to tell are the chronicler's judgement, so the passage shows how the survey looked to at least one writer of the time. Domesday Book itself never records that reaction.

misconceptions.feedback: Not even an ox, nor a cow, nor a swine is how a writer speaks when he wants to show how far the king went. It gives his impression, and the survey itself is the place to check what was listed.
The shame is the chronicler's. He sets it against the king, who he says thought it no shame, and the officials do not speak in the passage at all.

questions.prompt: A muster roll names 600 men able to fight in a town. A historian assumes that such men were between a fifth and a quarter of all the people. What is the largest population that fits her assumption?
hints: If the men were a fifth of the people, how many people were there for each man on the roll?
Work out the population under each assumption. Which share gives the larger town?
A fifth of the people means five people for every man named on the roll.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: If the 600 men were a fifth of the people, the town had 600 × 5 = 3,000. If they were a quarter, it had 600 × 4 = 2,400.

questions.onCorrect: The roll supports a range of 2,400 to 3,000 people, and the whole of that range comes from one assumption about who was left off the roll.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the population if the men were a quarter of the people. The smaller share gives the larger town.
That takes a share of the 600. The 600 are themselves the share, so the whole population is several times larger.

questions.prompt: In 1517 indulgences, papers promising release from punishment for sins, were being sold just before Luther wrote his Theses. Does being the last event before the Reformation make the sale its cause?
hints: What else had to be in place for a protest to spread?
Could the sale have done anything without those other factors?

acceptedIdeas: Not by timing alone, since it may only have set off what was already in place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not by timing alone, since it may only have set off what was already in place

questions.onCorrect: The last event before an outcome is often only the spark that set off conditions already in place.

misconceptions.feedback: Coming last is a matter of timing. The last event can be a spark that sets off conditions and causes which had been building for years.
Coming just before an outcome does not rule an event out as a cause, though it does not make it one either. Timing alone cannot settle the question.

choices.label: Yes, since the event just before an outcome is the one that produced it and nothing earlier did
No, since an event just before an outcome can never be counted as a cause of it
Not by timing alone, since it may only have set off what was already in place

questions.prompt: A bread riot broke out in a city on the morning the bakers raised their prices, and a historian lists five things that lay behind it. Which of the lesson's three kinds of factor is each one?
hints: Ask of each one how long it had been true, and whether it could have gone on being true without a riot.
Only one of the five happened at a single moment on the day itself.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dear bread and resentment of the governors are conditions, the preacher's argument and the guild's decision are causes, and the price rise that morning is the trigger.

items.label: Bread had been dear for years
items.explanation: It was in place for years without a riot, so it belongs to the background.

items.label: The city's governors had long been resented
items.explanation: Resentment that lasts for years makes a riot possible and does not start one.

items.label: For weeks a preacher had argued in the market that the price was a theft from the poor
items.explanation: An argument that changes minds pushes the outcome along, as Luther's did.

items.label: The weavers' guild had agreed to march if the price rose again
items.explanation: A decision to back the protest pushes it along, as the rulers who protected Luther did.

items.label: The bakers raised the price again that morning
items.explanation: It is the one event that set the riot off once everything else was in place.

questions.onCorrect: The trigger worked only because the conditions and the causes were already in place, which is why naming it alone explains so little.

questions.prompt: Which kind of factor was print in the Reformation?
hints: Did print produce Luther's argument, or carry it?
Compare what print did with the three definitions on the earlier screen.

acceptedIdeas: A condition, because it widened an audience without producing the argument
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A condition, because it widened an audience without producing the argument

questions.onCorrect: Print widened the audience for an argument it did not produce, which is the mark of a condition.

misconceptions.feedback: Print carried Luther's argument but did not produce it. A cause is a factor that actively drives the outcome, and the argument did that.
A trigger is one event that sets things off, and print had been in use for about sixty years before 1517.

choices.label: A cause, because it pushed the argument along and produced the whole movement
A trigger, because it set the protest off at a particular moment
A condition, because it widened an audience without producing the argument

questions.prompt: A chronicle records that a comet appeared in March and that the king died in April, and it concludes that the comet brought about his death. What is wrong with the reasoning?
hints: What does the chronicle offer to connect the two events, besides their order?
Think of the last event before the Reformation. What did the lesson say about timing alone?

acceptedIdeas: It takes an earlier event for a cause with no link shown
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It takes an earlier event for a cause with no link shown

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since the cause came before the effect
It takes an earlier event for a cause with no link shown
It is a chronicle, so nothing in it can be relied upon

questions.onCorrect: Order in time shows which event could have caused the other and nothing more. A cause needs a link, and a counterfactual test asks whether the king would have died without the comet.

misconceptions.feedback: Coming first is needed for a cause and is far from enough. Many things happened in March, and the chronicle shows no link between this one and the death.
The chronicle may be right about both dates. The fault lies in the step from one event to the other, and throwing out the whole source would lose the dates as well.

questions.prompt: A historian doubts that a city fell because its walls were weak. She imagines the walls repaired, keeps everything else as it was, and asks whether the city would still have fallen. What is this kind of test called?
hints: She reasons about something that did not happen.
The lesson used the same test on printing: remove one factor in thought and ask whether the outcome still seems likely.

acceptedIdeas: counterfactual
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: counterfactual

questions.onCorrect: A counterfactual removes or changes one factor in thought. Its answer is a judgement of likelihood, so it supports an argument and settles nothing alone.

misconceptions.feedback: A trigger is an event that sets something off. This question describes a test.

questions.prompt: "Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476." What kind of claim is this?
hints: Could a source show this statement to be wrong?
Does it say what the event meant, or only that it happened?

acceptedIdeas: A fact claim, which sources can confirm or correct
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fact claim, which sources can confirm or correct

questions.onCorrect: A fact claim names a dated event that sources can confirm or correct.

misconceptions.feedback: Being written later does not make a claim an interpretation. This one says that a named event happened at a date, and sources can check that.
Nobody alive saw most of history, yet sources can still confirm or correct a date and an event, which is what makes this a fact claim.

choices.label: A fact claim, which sources can confirm or correct
An opinion, since no one alive today saw it happen
An interpretation, since historians wrote it down long afterwards

questions.prompt:
Edward Gibbon, in *The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire*, on what Christianity did to the empire.

> The clergy successfully preached the doctrines of patience and pusillanimity: the active virtues of society were discouraged; and the last remains of military spirit were buried in the cloister

Which of the lesson's three kinds of statement is this sentence?
hints: Which words in the sentence are judgements?
Could two historians accept every sermon as genuine and still disagree with this sentence?

acceptedIdeas: interpretation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: interpretation

questions.onCorrect: Pusillanimity, discouraged and buried are Gibbon's judgements about cause and effect. The sentence is also evidence of something else, which is how an eighteenth-century writer weighed Christianity against civic and military virtue.

misconceptions.feedback: That the clergy preached patience could be checked in surviving sermons. The sentence goes further and says what the preaching did to society and to the army, and no single source could confirm that.
Evidence is the material a reading rests on, such as coins or pottery. This sentence is the reading itself, in Gibbon's words.

questions.prompt: As Ward-Perkins uses it, which of the three kinds of statement is 'Fine pottery disappears from much of Britain in the fifth century'?
hints: Ask what Ward-Perkins does with the statement.
Ask whether it says what the pottery means or only reports it.

acceptedIdeas: Evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Evidence

questions.onCorrect: Evidence is what a historian offers in support of a reading, and it can be challenged on whether it is typical.

misconceptions.feedback: It can be checked, as a fact claim can, but here it is offered in support of a reading, and that use is what the kinds of statement are sorted by.
An interpretation says what the facts mean or why they happened. The pottery statement says neither: it is the material a reading is built on.

choices.label: Evidence
A fact claim
An interpretation

questions.prompt: A historian writes a book comparing how Gibbon, Brown and Ward-Perkins framed the end of Rome, and how each one's questions reflected his own time. What is the study her book belongs to called?
hints: Her sources are earlier historians.
The word has history and writing in it.

acceptedIdeas: historiography
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: historiography

questions.onCorrect: Historiography treats earlier historians as evidence of their own time.

questions.prompt:
Gibbon also gives a general explanation of Rome's fall.

> But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness. Prosperity ripened the principle of decay; the causes of destruction multiplied with the extent of conquest

Which finding would count most against this reading?
hints: What does the reading say that size does to an empire?
What would you expect never to find if size made decline inevitable?

acceptedIdeas: Large empires that lasted far longer without declining
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Large empires that lasted far longer without declining

choices.label: A source that gives a new date for the fall of the West
Large empires that lasted far longer without declining
A letter showing that Gibbon admired the Roman republic

questions.onCorrect: The reading says that greatness itself brings decline, so great empires that endured would cut against it. The eastern Roman state, which lasted until 1453, is a case it has to explain.

misconceptions.feedback: A corrected date would change a fact claim. Gibbon's reading is about why Rome declined, and it would survive a new date untouched.
Gibbon's tastes may explain why he asked his question. A reading is tested against evidence about the past, and his admiration leaves the Roman evidence where it was.

questions.prompt: A history book of 1900 praises or blames each medieval king by one test, whether he would have made a good ruler in 1900, and its author never notices that he is doing so. What is this fault called?
hints: Whose standards is the author using?
The lesson named the habit of reading the past through the concerns of one's own day.

acceptedIdeas: presentism
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: presentism

questions.onCorrect: Presentism is a risk for every age, and the cure is to state our questions and ask whether the people we study would have recognised them.

misconceptions.feedback: Every author has a point of view. The lesson has a narrower name for judging the past by the standards of the author's own day.

questions.prompt: A historian writes about a city between 1340 and 1360, and six sentences from her chapter are listed here. Which of the lesson's three kinds of statement is each one?
hints: Ask of each sentence whether a source could simply confirm it, whether it points to material offered in support, or whether it says what the facts meant.
Two of the sentences name the records the historian is relying on.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The loss of half the people and the end of the council's meetings are fact claims, the tax rolls and the building accounts are evidence, and catastrophe and opportunity are interpretations.

items.label: The city lost half its people between 1340 and 1360.
items.explanation: It says that something happened, and a better source could confirm or correct it.

items.label: The city council stopped meeting in 1349.
items.explanation: It names a dated event that the council's own records could confirm.

items.label: The tax rolls list 4,100 households in 1340 and 2,050 in 1360, which is how the loss is known.
items.explanation: She offers the rolls as the material that supports her figure.

items.label: Building accounts show a labourer's daily wage doubling by 1360, which supports the view that survivors gained.
items.explanation: The accounts are offered in support of a reading, and we can ask whether they are typical.

items.label: Those twenty years were a catastrophe for the city.
items.explanation: Catastrophe is a judgement about what the loss meant, to be weighed against rival readings.

items.label: For those who lived, it was a time of opportunity.
items.explanation: It says what the same facts meant, and a historian who accepts every figure can still dispute it.

questions.onCorrect: The two interpretations rest on the same facts, so the dispute between them is about meaning, and each can be tested by how much of the evidence it covers.

questions.prompt: To be disseised was to be put out of one's land, and in 1215 free men were a minority of the people of England. Whom did the clause protect when it was sealed?

extracts.text: No freemen shall be taken or imprisoned or disseised or exiled or in any way destroyed, nor will we go upon him nor send upon him, except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land.
extracts.when: sealed by King John in June 1215
extracts.kind: A charter drawn up after rebel barons rose against the king

hints: Read the first two words of the clause.
Who was a free man in 1215, and who was left outside the words?

acceptedIdeas: Free men alone, who were a minority of the people of England
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free men alone, who were a minority of the people of England

choices.label: Every person in England, since it speaks of the law of the land
Free men alone, who were a minority of the people of England
The barons alone, since they had forced the king to seal it

questions.onCorrect: The clause covered free men, who were a minority. Reading it as a promise to everyone puts a later idea into 1215.

misconceptions.feedback: The law of the land is how a free man was to be judged. The clause names who is covered in its first two words, and most people in 1215 were not free in the law's sense.
The barons forced the charter, yet this clause speaks of freemen, a wider group than the barons. It still left out everyone who was unfree.

questions.prompt: Many people picture Magna Carta, the charter King John sealed at Runnymede in 1215, as a statement of the rights of every English person. What was it in 1215?
hints: Who had risen against the king, and what did they want?
Whom did the words free man cover?

acceptedIdeas: A settlement between King John and rebel barons, for free men only
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A settlement between King John and rebel barons, for free men only

questions.onCorrect: It answered the grievances of barons against a king, and its protections reached only the free.

misconceptions.feedback: Its protections reached the free, who were only some of the people in England, and it answered the complaints of barons who had risen against the king.
The pope's part came afterwards, when he declared the charter void in August 1215. The charter itself was sealed by John after the barons rose against him.

choices.label: A ruling by the pope on the king's quarrel with the barons
A settlement between King John and rebel barons, for free men only
A statement of the rights of every English person, whether free or unfree

questions.prompt: A film shows the barons at Runnymede in 1215 demanding the vote for every English man and woman. What do we call that kind of error?
hints: It is a mistake about time.
Did anyone in 1215 think in those terms?

acceptedIdeas: anachronism
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: anachronism

questions.onCorrect: Anachronism matters most where a document has been famous for a long time and its later meanings are easy to read backwards.

questions.prompt: A peace treaty broke down within a year, but diplomats cited it as a model for the next century. What can a historian say about its significance?
hints: Ask what question is being put to the treaty.
Ask whether one answer could hold for every question.

acceptedIdeas: It depends on the question: slight for its own year, large for later diplomacy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It depends on the question: slight for its own year, large for later diplomacy

questions.onCorrect: Significance depends on the question, and later use is part of a document's afterlife.

misconceptions.feedback: Asking only whether the treaty kept the peace leaves out what happened to it afterwards. Significance is relative to the question asked.
Later use matters for questions about later times. For a question about the treaty's own year, a failure within twelve months counts for a lot.

choices.label: It had none, since a treaty that broke down within a year settled nothing at all
It was large, since how a treaty is used later is the only measure
It depends on the question: slight for its own year, large for later diplomacy

questions.prompt: In 1628 the English Parliament addressed the Petition of Right to Charles I, and one of its clauses repeats the charter of 1215 almost word for word. What is Source B evidence of?

extracts.text: No freemen shall be taken or imprisoned or disseised or exiled or in any way destroyed, nor will we go upon him nor send upon him, except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land.
extracts.when: sealed by King John in June 1215

extracts.who: The Petition of Right, clause III
extracts.kind: A petition from the English Parliament to Charles I

hints: Who is speaking in Source B, and in which year?
Which part of the charter's history do the 1620s belong to?

acceptedIdeas: How Parliament used the charter against a king in 1628
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How Parliament used the charter against a king in 1628

choices.label: What the barons at Runnymede meant by the charter in 1215
How Parliament used the charter against a king in 1628
That the charter had protected every subject since 1215

questions.onCorrect: Source B shows the charter at work in 1628, quoted as law against Charles I. That use belongs to its afterlife and tells us about the 1620s.

misconceptions.feedback: Source B was written four centuries after Runnymede by men with a quarrel of their own. For what the barons meant we need evidence from 1215, such as Source A.
Source B claims the charter as standing law, which served Parliament's case. The charter's first life ended within ten weeks, and its words covered free men only.

questions.prompt: The reissues of the charter, the lawyers who cited it in the 1620s and the people who quote it today all belong to one part of Magna Carta's history, the part that came after 1215. What does the lesson call that part?
hints: It is the story of what later people did with the document.
The lesson set it against what the charter did in its own time.

acceptedIdeas: afterlife
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: afterlife

questions.onCorrect: A document's afterlife is real history, but it does not tell us what its makers meant.

questions.prompt: Most of the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue left no writing of their own. What does that tell us about their views and actions?
hints: Why did few of the enslaved leave writing?
Is a gap in the record a fact about the people or about the record?

acceptedIdeas: Nothing directly, since it describes the record and not the people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing directly, since it describes the record and not the people

questions.onCorrect: Having left no writing says something about the record. It says nothing about whether people thought or acted.

misconceptions.feedback: Leaving no writing reflects who had the chance to learn to read and write. The uprising itself, made by the enslaved at great scale, shows people acting on their own views.
The uprising began among the enslaved and was carried on by them for years. A thin written record measures who held the pens, and it does not measure who acted.

choices.label: That their part in the revolution was small, as the record suggests
Nothing directly, since it describes the record and not the people
That they had few views of their own and followed their leaders

questions.prompt: Landless labourers in eighteenth-century France appear in the records mostly when officials taxed, counted or arrested them. What word do historians use for a group in that position?
hints: The word names a position outside the structures of power.
The lesson used it for the enslaved majority of Saint-Domingue.

acceptedIdeas: subaltern
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: subaltern

questions.onCorrect: Subaltern is a reminder that a large record can still be a lopsided one.

questions.prompt: A factory owner's rule book fines workers for singing, for talking and for leaving their machines. No writing by the workers survives. Read against the grain, what does the rule book suggest?
hints: Why would an owner write a rule against something?
What did the planter's notice show that the planter never meant to say?

acceptedIdeas: That workers sang, talked and left often enough to be fined
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That workers sang, talked and left often enough to be fined

choices.label: That the workers kept silent and stayed at their machines all day
That workers sang, talked and left often enough to be fined
Nothing about the workers, since the owner wrote the rules

questions.onCorrect: A rule against singing is evidence that people sang. The owner meant to record his authority, and he recorded his workers' habits as well.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the rules as a description of what happened. Rules are written against things people do, so they point the other way.
The owner's purpose was to control his workers, and that is why the rules are useful. They record, without meaning to, what he was trying to stop.

questions.prompt:
In his memoir Toussaint Louverture describes the colony under his command.

> The colony of Saint Domingo, of which I was commander, enjoyed the greatest tranquillity; agriculture and commerce flourished there. The island had attained a degree of splendor which it had never before seen.

A historian wants to know how the people who worked the plantations found those years. How far does this passage take her?
hints: Whose point of view is tranquillity and flourishing commerce?
Would a field worker have measured those years by the colony's trade?

acceptedIdeas: A short way, since it gives a commander's view of the colony
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A short way, since it gives a commander's view of the colony

choices.label: All the way, since he had once worked the land himself
A short way, since it gives a commander's view of the colony
Nowhere, since a man praising his own rule proves nothing at all

questions.onCorrect: The passage tells her what the commander counted as success. For the workers' experience she has to read other records against the grain and look for evidence they left themselves.

misconceptions.feedback: His past gave him knowledge that a planter lacked. Here he writes as commander, to defend his record, and he reports the colony's output and says nothing of how the work felt.
Self-praise is a reason to test the passage against other records. It still shows what he counted as success, and that is worth knowing.

questions.prompt: Songs still sung in a village tell of a flood that no document records. What do historians call evidence that is carried by speech in this way?
hints: It is named after the way it was carried from one generation to the next.
The lesson set it beside written evidence, as different and no worse.

acceptedIdeas: oral evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: oral evidence

questions.onCorrect: Oral evidence can preserve what writing did not, and it changes in the telling, so we still ask who told it, to whom and when.

misconceptions.feedback: Subaltern names the groups that the written record leaves out. The question asks for the kind of evidence, which is named after the way it is passed on.

questions.prompt: Someone claims that Britain's entry into the war pushed Austria-Hungary to attack Serbia. In what order did these five events of 1914 happen?
hints: Start with the event that came five weeks before the fighting spread, and end with the declaration that followed German troops entering Belgium.
Germany's two declarations came between Austria-Hungary's and Britain's. Which of the two did the screen before this one date to 1 August?

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shooting at Sarajevo on 28 June came first. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, Germany on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and Britain on Germany on 4 August.

items: Franz Ferdinand is shot at Sarajevo

questions.onCorrect: Britain's declaration came last, a week after Austria-Hungary's, so it cannot have pushed Austria-Hungary to act. Order can rule a cause out and can never rule one in.

questions.prompt: On 28 June 1914 Franz Ferdinand was shot at Sarajevo, and five weeks later the great powers were at war. Is the assassination alone enough to explain that war?
hints: What happened in the five weeks between the shooting and the war?
Could one shooting, with nothing else in place, set the great powers against one another?

acceptedIdeas: No, since it needed years of rivalry and weeks of government decisions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since it needed years of rivalry and weeks of government decisions

questions.onCorrect: The war needed years of rivalry in place and weeks of decisions by governments to follow the spark.

misconceptions.feedback: Following in time does not explain. Between the shooting and the war came five weeks of choices by governments, and behind them years of alliances and arms races.

Even if a war in 1914 needed the shooting, the shooting needed other things to become a war between great powers: alliances, an arms race and the decisions of July. A factor can be necessary without being enough.

choices.label: Yes, since the war followed directly from the shooting and from nothing else
No, since it needed years of rivalry and weeks of government decisions
Yes, since without the shooting there would have been no war that summer or later

questions.prompt: Two states had been arming against each other for years, and war came three days after a border guard was shot. In the terms of this lesson and the Reformation lesson, what was the shooting?
hints: It was not a pressure built over years or a decision of the crisis.
It set things off at one moment.

acceptedIdeas: trigger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: trigger

questions.onCorrect: A trigger works only because the long-term pressures and short-term decisions are in place to carry it along.

misconceptions.feedback: A condition is the background, such as the years of arming. The shooting is the event that set the war off.
A short-term cause is a decision made during the crisis itself. The shooting came first and set the crisis going.

questions.prompt: Which kind of factor were the demands that Austria-Hungary sent to Serbia on 23 July 1914?
hints: Did it act over years or over weeks?
Compare it with a pressure that builds over years and an event that starts the crisis.

acceptedIdeas: A short-term cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A short-term cause

questions.onCorrect: A decision made in the weeks of the crisis is a short-term cause, which sits between the long-term pressures and the trigger.

misconceptions.feedback: The trigger was the shooting at Sarajevo, the event that set the crisis off. Austria-Hungary's demands came nearly four weeks later, as a choice made in response.
A long-term cause builds over years. These demands were sent in the fourth week of the crisis.

choices.label: A short-term cause
The trigger of the war
A long-term cause

questions.prompt: Which one-line claim about the causes of the war of 1914 is specific enough to be argued and qualified enough to be fair?
hints: Which claim names its factors and says how they worked?
Which one could be shown wrong by evidence?

acceptedIdeas: Rival alliances turned a Balkan crisis into a general war, though July's decisions mattered as much
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rival alliances turned a Balkan crisis into a general war, though July's decisions mattered as much

choices.label: Once Europe had split into two armed camps, a general war could no longer have been avoided by anyone
Rival alliances turned a Balkan crisis into a general war, though July's decisions mattered as much
Many different factors caused the war, and historians weigh each one of them differently
A single assassination at Sarajevo caused the war, since nothing else that summer decided it

questions.onCorrect: A good claim names its factors, says how they worked and admits what it leaves out.

misconceptions.feedback: A war that was likely was not therefore bound to come. The choices of the crisis could have gone differently.
This is too broad to be wrong, so it says almost nothing. A claim should be narrow enough to argue with.
One assassin cannot explain why a shooting became a general war. This claim ignores the pressures and the decisions.

questions.prompt: A village rose in revolt, and a historian has found five things that lay behind it. How should she sort them by the time over which each one acted?
hints: How long had each one been acting when the revolt began?
Only one of the five happened at a single moment.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The drought and the old quarrel are long-term causes, the tax and the refused petition are short-term causes, and the bailiff's blow is the trigger.

items.label: A drought that had lasted ten years
items.explanation: Ten years of poor harvests built the pressure without starting a revolt on any one day.

items.label: A quarrel over the common land that went back a generation
items.explanation: A grievance a generation old is a pressure built over years, like the alliances before 1914.

items.label: A grain tax announced that spring
items.explanation: It was a decision made a few months before the revolt, as the crisis took shape.

items.label: The lord's refusal, that week, to hear the villagers' petition
items.explanation: It was a choice made in the last days, and a different choice might have calmed the village.

items.label: A bailiff striking a farmer on the morning the revolt began
items.explanation: It happened at one moment and set off what the other four had prepared.

questions.onCorrect: The three levels depend on one another: the blow mattered because years of pressure and that spring's decisions stood behind it.

questions.prompt: A historian writes that the war of 1914 turned on choices made in July, any of which could have gone another way. What word does the lesson use for that idea?
hints: It is the opposite of saying that the war was bound to come.
The lesson introduced the word when it asked whether a long list of causes made war inevitable.

acceptedIdeas: contingency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: contingency

questions.onCorrect: Contingency is why a likely war was not an inevitable one.

questions.prompt: Could any evidence show the claim "Industrialisation had many causes" to be wrong?
hints: Imagine any finding at all. Would the claim still be true?
Does the claim name a factor or say how it worked?

acceptedIdeas: No, since it commits to nothing that evidence could contradict
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since it commits to nothing that evidence could contradict

choices.label: Yes, if some of the causes turned out to be unimportant
Yes, if historians found that one single cause had mattered most of all
No, since it commits to nothing that evidence could contradict

questions.onCorrect: A claim that is safe from every possible finding commits to nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: If some causes were unimportant, others would still be there, and the claim would still stand. Whatever evidence turns up, it survives, which is why it says nothing.
If one cause mattered most, there would still be others, so the claim would survive. It names no cause and no weight, so nothing could contradict it.

questions.prompt: Which finding would count against the claim that high wages made machines pay?
hints: The claim says high wages made machines pay.
Which finding would a believer in the claim not expect to see?

acceptedIdeas: Machines were first adopted where wages were low
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Machines were first adopted where wages were low

questions.onCorrect: If machines first appeared where wages were low, the link between high wages and mechanisation would be in doubt.

misconceptions.feedback: Cheap coal is the other half of the claim, so this finding fits it.
Better machines are consistent with the claim and say nothing about wages.
Rising wages where machines spread fit the claim, since it links high wages to machines paying.

choices.label: Machines were first adopted where coal was cheap
Machines became more efficient over the century
Machines were first adopted where wages were low
Wages rose in the towns where machines spread

questions.prompt: Some historians argue that overseas trade drove Britain's early industrialisation. Which finding would most weaken that claim?
hints: What does the claim say should be true?
Which finding says the opposite?

acceptedIdeas: Industry grew fastest in regions with little overseas trade
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Industry grew fastest in regions with little overseas trade

choices.label: Steam engines became more efficient after 1769, thanks to James Watt
Britain had a large merchant fleet
British exports rose during the eighteenth century
Industry grew fastest in regions with little overseas trade

questions.onCorrect: Counter-evidence points the other way from the link the claim proposes.

misconceptions.feedback: A large merchant fleet is what the claim would lead us to expect, so it supports the claim.
Better engines are consistent with the claim and do not bear on trade.
Rising exports would support the claim and not weaken it.

questions.prompt: A historian rewrites the claim that coal caused industrialisation. Her new version says that cheap coal was the main reason industry grew early in Britain. What does the lesson call words such as main and in Britain, which mark how far a claim reaches?
hints: They mark the edge of what the evidence supports.
The lesson set the word beside hedge, and said the two are different.

acceptedIdeas: qualification
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: qualification

questions.onCorrect: A qualification marks where the evidence ends, and makes the claim exact.

questions.prompt: A historian claims that a famine was caused mainly by drought. She then finds that the district which suffered most had normal rainfall that year. What does the lesson call a finding of this kind?
hints: Does the finding point the same way as her claim?
The lesson said a careful historian names this kind of evidence in advance.

acceptedIdeas: counter-evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: counter-evidence

questions.onCorrect: A good historian names the counter-evidence and says what it does to the claim.

questions.prompt: Drawn in proportion, the course's nine cases are unevenly spaced: four fall before 500 CE, and three fall in the four centuries before 1914. What does the spacing show?
hints: Who decided which nine events went on the line?
Would a different course have drawn the same line?

Which cases the course chose to study, and little more
That events came faster as the modern age drew nearer to 1914

More cases from recent centuries reflects where the course looked. A timeline of chosen cases cannot measure how much happened in any period.

questions.prompt: What did the authors of these three records have in common?
hints: Ask who held the pens in each case.
Ask what kind of person each author was.

acceptedIdeas: They were all people with power or standing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They were all people with power or standing

misconceptions.feedback: An emperor, a king's officials and planters were not ordinary people recording daily life.
These records were made at the time of the events, not long after them.

choices.label: They were all ordinary people recording daily life
They were all people with power or standing
They were all writing long after the events

acceptedIdeas: A claim about this revolution, which other cases could then test
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A claim about this revolution, which other cases could then test

choices.label: A claim about all of them, since she studied this case so closely
A claim about this revolution, which other cases could then test
Nothing at all, since a single case is never evidence

questions.prompt: Six of the course's cases are listed here without their dates. In what order did they happen?
